maintopic: COMMUNICATIONS AND CULTURE-FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present the fourth report of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, in both official languages. Our study and recommendations are based on the annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for 1985-86. Our Committee requests that the Government table a response to this report, pursuant to Standing Order 99(2).
The Committee examined the circumstances that prevented the Auditor General from completing the audit of CBC books. In presenting its findings and recommendations, the Committee wishes to help define solutions to CBC problems.

The committee's report reaffirms the importance of the CBC in Canadian broadcasting and expresses agreement with the Caplan-Sauvageau Task Force that it is upon the CBC that we must rely for an abundance of compelling radio and television programs by, for and about Canadians.
The committee regards the CBC's accounting problems as a serious matter because they resulted in CBC's management being unable to provide a full accounting to its board of directors and, as a result, prevented the corporation from giving Parliament a reliable account of its expenditures. Our hearings raised issues related to the financial management and accountability of the CBC and, specifically, the role and responsibilities of the CBC's board of directors, its audit committee, internal auditor and president.
Thus the committee recommends immediate amendments to the Broadcasting Act to clarify the role and responsibility of the CBC's board, the audit committee and the internal auditor; to expand on the rights and duties of the Auditor General; and to provide separately for a chairman of the board and a president.

I take this opportunity to thank the representatives of all three parties for their sustained efforts in drafting this unanimous report to the House. The results of our work prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that parliamentary reform is a success.

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, February 16, consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall that Bill C-38, an Act respecting the reorganization and divestiture of Teleglobe Canada, be now read the second time and referred to a legislative committee, and the amendment of Ms. McDonald (p. 3435).

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to Bill C-38, especially since yesterday, my hon. friend from the riding next door, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) who is in the House today, rose in the House to express the hope I would speak to this Bill.

February 17, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
Mr. Speaker, as you know, I was a Member of the Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons, and at the time I was in the Opposition. Now we all know that the Opposition always criticizes whatever the Government does, but when it forms the Government it insists everything is all right. The Hon. Member will recall that when his Government was in power, it tabled a Bill whose purpose was to privatize Teleglobe Canada. It was a good idea at the time, but today it is no longer a good idea. They are looking for all kinds of excuses to call this a bad idea, because they are now in the Opposition. However, when they were on this side of the House, when they were the Government, there were no objections to selling the corporation. And now we are finally proceeding with privatization, they suddenly come up with all kinds of reasons why it no longer makes sense.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: What a shame.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
What a shame indeed. Mr. Speaker, I would like to say, for the benefit of those who are not aware of the fact, that the overseas facilities are located in Weir, in the beautiful riding of	Argenteuil-Papineau.	Seventeen
employees work there in a magnificient setting and excellent working conditions, since they are using the very latest technology which is a real challenge for them. In fact, Teleglobe receives hundreds of Canadian visitors during the summer, who come every year to travel around this beautiful part of my riding. According to the statistics, it seems quite a few of these visitors later decided to buy a lot or a cottage because the area is so beautiful people can't help but invest their money there. I would invite Hon. Members to come and visit. In fact, the Hon. Member for Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault) is familiar with the area because his wife lives nearby.
Mr. Speaker, the Government would have lost its credibility by only selling Crown corporations that were not making a profit. People tend to want to get rid of the bad stuff and keep the good stuff. I believe that if the Government is to be credible, it must sell all Crown corporations according to the schedule agreed on by the Government and the Minister of State (Privatization) (Mrs. McDougall).
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that in most Opposition ridings, constituents agree with our plan to privatize Crown corporations. Mr. Speaker, there are those who object and say: Why sell the one that happens to be the most profitable Crown corporation? Mr. Speaker, simply because Teleglobe has a monopoly on international communications in Canada and because in the long run, a monopoly position can only have an adverse effect on profits and efficiency. We know that in Canada, efficiency and profits are at a very low ebb, and that is not good for our companies.
Furthermore, considering that five years from now, the market will be opened up for competition, it was essential to start by privatizing the existing monopoly. Mr. Speaker, can any business compete with a Government-supported company? Now that Teleglobe has been sold to Memotec, it will no
longer pay dividends to the Government, but it will now have to pay federal and provincial income tax as well as all the local taxes, like any other business. I, for one, believe that as a result, there will be a better distribution of the corporation's profits.
There is another objection that is always raised. It is that a country's international communications have strategic importance and thus cannot be sold off to the private sector. Mr. Speaker, a case could have been made during the war, but the argument is no longer valid at this time, when individuals and especially businesses are increasingly using a service that has now become strictly commercial. It is no longer a matter of military considerations. And so, there is no justification for having a state monopoly on what is almost exclusively a telephone service.
What counts for my constituents is lower overseas rates and the knowledge they will be protected from now on by the CRTC. Mr. Speaker, do you think Canadians will buy the Opposition's arguments, especially those made by the New Democratic Party, which would like to see the Government own more, not fewer businesses? Where will the money and the taxes come from? I have some constituents who are saying they wished the tax reform would be put through, because it is getting very expensive to pay for all this. There is no need for that, Mr. Speaker. There is no need for the Government to own private businesses.
This became quite obvious during the electoral campaign. Our constituents gave us a very clear message: Please, get out of private business. See to it that the taxpayers' money is fairly and adequately administered instead of wasting your time with business activities when you are not in competition with the private sector. This is what the Progressive Conservative government has done. We had promised that we would do so and we are doing it.
Do you not think that this is a unique and fantastic opportunity for Memotec, a young and dynamic Montreal business with everything going for it, which did not hesitate to offer more than all the other bidders? This is Quebec entrepreneurship. I congratulate the management and the employees of Memotec on this deal and I am glad to know that big businesses are not the only ones able to purchase Crown corporations and other large companies.
Memotec is certainly not as big as Bell, Power Corporation or other large companies. It is a young, growing business cased on risk capital and with serious shareholders, such as the Deposit and Investment Fund, and on the pension funds of public servants financed by the National Bank. Memotec has more to offer and it limits its operations to communications. I am convinced that, with the way Canadian broadcasting and telecommunications are controlled, the risk of conflict of interests in this company will be minimal, I therefore congratulate Memotec. I met its president when the sale was announced and he was very enthusiastic. Naturally, what I was most interested in knowing was whether there would be more
February 17, 1987

jobs in Weir, for instance, in my constituency. Of course, that is what these people want.
In the last two years, I have often visited that part of my constituency and I remember meeting the employees of the company last summer. Naturally, they were a bit worried about losing what benefits they had then if the Government sold Teleglobe. On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, they will now be able to purchase shares at very favourable conditions. They will have a pension plan comparable to the public service plan and their jobs have been guaranteed. Indeed, if I may emphasize this point, under the special provisions related to the workers, Teleglobe employees will continue to come under federal jurisdiction as concerns the Labour Code and all existing collective agreements will continue to apply. As I said earlier, Memotec has offered to current employees of Teleglobe a pension plan similar to that of federal public servants.
A special provision has also been made to establish a shareholding plan for employees. This offer involves 5 per cent of shares and provides a 10 per cent discount on the purchase price. Employees who wish to apply can also obtain an interest-free loan. I would like to say that I am happy for the people of my constituency who will be able to benefit from this sale.
Last Sunday, we saw on the French network of the CBC the Gemeaux Awards which reward excellence in radio and television programs. Awards should also be given to private businesses such as Memotec since its partnership with Teleglobe is the best way in my opinion to guarantee a great future for communications in Canada, which will be of great benefit to Canadian consumers.

more having been consistent with its policies, for having sold Teleglobe to a young Quebec corporation with headquarters in Montreal. Mr. Speaker, I say bravo for this Government.

As you know, they have decided what place or rank they give this Government in public opinion pools and whether or not it deserves such congratulations as those the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau referred to a little while ago.
In her speech, the Hon. Member was saying that a Crown corporation, in view of its very structure, was unable to compete effectively because, before making a decision, a whole slew of Government officials had to be involved through the chain of command and because of this process, the Government had to divest itself of Crown corporations.

I suggest that the Government should consider the possible divestiture of a Crown corporation only after it has ascertained that it no longer meets its political objectives; in other words, when an industry serves a national policy the preservation of a Crown corporation is necessary to meet these objectives. In such a case, there should be no divestiture. If a corporation is failing, if its structure must be changed, then the Government should change it, but keep it when it serves the public interest.
Therefore, I ask the Hon. Mr. Speaker, I must begin by making a brief comment on the speech of the Hon. Member. She made a great point of the fact that the Government was being responsible by not selling this firm to a foreign company. I must say that those are sentiments with which I agree, but I wonder if this same sentiment applied to the purchase of de Havilland by Boeing which occurred earlier this year. We have seen clear cases of the Government attempting to find a bidder which turned out to be a foreign purchaser. The Government has expressed not only no apology for doing so but pride in managing to attract to Canada a grand foreign firm that would be the salvation of a particular Crown corporation. The Government cannot have it both ways.
It must accept either that it considers the ownership of a company to which it is selling a Crown corporation as important or it is not important. It cannot try to play both ends against the middle as evidenced by the Hon. Member's comments.
I would like to try to analyse this sale and show that it is somehow typical and a sign to the country of what privatization Conservative-style will mean. There is a very easy acceptance in Canada that it makes sense to sell off assets which have been built up over many years and which have fulfilled important public purposes for the sake of short-term economic returns. It seems to me that this case gives us very serious pause to reconsider that acceptance. I would hope it will force the Canadian people to raise questions that will affect not only this sale but the entire thrust of the Government's efforts to get rid of what is, after all, the historical legacy the people of Canada have built up over the years.
We must begin by asking if we have here a case of a whale being swallowed by a minnow. An extremely small firm that in its annual revenue had only something in the order of $31 million, which it received during the first nine months of 1986, is purchasing an extremely huge firm. It is purchasing this firm, not with its own money, not with money that it had somehow accumulated through a share issue to Canadians, but with money from bank loans and debentures. That is a very, very profitable way to purchase and take over another company. That is because the profits of the company compared to the actual equity invested are extremely large. It is also an extremely risky way to do a takeover.
[DOT] (U50)
This is exactly the kind of predatory takeover which has led people to talk, not about minnows taking over whales but sharks taking over whales. They then carve up the carcass, selling off bits and pieces and generally demolishing the company and its future prospects. I am not suggesting that that will necessarily take place in this case, but it smacks very much of that kind of approach to financing. It is not yet commonplace in Canada and I hope it never becomes commonplace. However, this kind of sell-out is likely to encourage the same kind of thing. It can be very devastating for the

February 17, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
private companies who experience it and I regret that is the approach taken.
The second reality we have to deal with is that even in the case of a Crown corporation which was very easy to sell, the Government still could not do it properly and competently. On the very day that the decision, a supposed secret, was announced, the shares of Memotec started to sky-rocket on the stock exchange. They went up a total of $2.38, over 20 per cent. After that Memotec announced it had an interest in taking over Teleglobe. It is very clear that there was a leak of information.
Once more we have gross incompetence demonstrated by the Government in the process it used. That is unfortunately all too typical of the Government. That is the scandal which the Member who spoke previously was unprepared to recognize. It cannot be sloughed off to the side because it involves incompetency and, I must say, dishonesty. Clearly people with insider information bought shares in Memotec when no one else had heard of that little minnow in the economic community. They bought the shares and pushed the price up by 20 per cent and, I suggest, made a tremendous and unconscionable financial killing, I hope it will rest heavily on their consciences in the future. This is a classic case of incompetence of which no Government should be guilty.
We also have to recognize there has been a tremendous effort to throw up a great smoke-screen over the price of Teleglobe so the Government can say it got a tremendous price. It has been suggested that over $600 million was poured into the Government's coffers by this deal. The Financial Post, hardly a paragon of socialist economics, after a careful analysis indicated quite clearly that the price paid is only $345 million. Once again the Government demonstrates not only its incompetence but its congenital incapacity to be forthright with the people of Canada. That is the third reality demonstrated by this sell off.
There has also been the suggestion that this deal provides protection to the consumer. All of us in this place have a tremendous concern about consumer protection. Yet nowhere in this deal is there any evidence of protection for the consumer. We have instead a five-year monopoly given to this corporate minnow so it can make as much money as possible. It is not doing that with its own money but with the bank's money. Memotec will do very well. At the end of the five-year monopoly it will likely sell the company, carve it up and give the various telephone companies a piece. It will have done handsomely without making any contribution whatsoever to the economic prosperity and well-being of Canada.
In addition to the five-year monopoly the Government has promised to bring in legislation to prevent competition involving communication lines running through Canada and those running through the U.S. The Government talks about competition and consumer protection, yet it creates a five-year monopoly and promises to eliminate certain competition through legislation.
*
It is not just those of us on the opposition side of the House who raise questions about this sale. The union representing the company in question has suggested that tremendous risk for Teleglobe is embodied in this sale. Again, the minnow swallowing the whale is apt to get indigestion. In addition, there is absolutely nothing in the legislation which demonstrates a guarantee of any sort for the workers in the company that their jobs are in any sense secure. At least there was some suggestion of that in previous privatizations. According to the unions, there is a probability that there will be lay-offs in the future in Teleglobe.
This is privatization Conservative style. It is ill-thought through. It is inconsistent. It is incompetently put into effect. It is dishonest with respect to the price which is actually being announced, and it has established monopolistic, uncompetitive conditions while it trumpets about competition to all and sundry.
That kind of approach has brought the Conservative Party to a position where only 23 per cent of the people of the country are prepared to vote for it. It is unfortunate that a Government which was elected with so much promise should have brought itself to that position, but it is completely and utterly understandable that that should be where it stands when its modus operandi, its approach to even such a simple, straightforward sale as that of Teleglobe, should be so marked by incompetence and lack of thought about what was being undertaken.
We suggest that the Government think again, that it take three months, that it allow itself, as it has claimed is its responsibility, to investigate the insider trading charge which has been made on the various stock exchanges. After such investigation is undertaken and assurances are provided to the workers in this enterprise, the Government should return to the House with a revised Bill with more honesty and more competence than it has demonstrated in this case.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw attention to three points made in the Hon. Member's address. He dwells upon the smallness of the purchaser as if there were something wrong with that. One could infer that he might have been in favour of the purchase had the purchaser been large. I had to wonder whether he would have voted for it if the buyer had been Northern Telecom or some other large corporation. The real test should be the price offered to the public and the ability of the company to pay it. There is a good side to the company being small. Do we not want to give smaller enterprises an opportunity to build themselves up and progress in the interests of Canada?
Second, the Member dwelt upon the leak of information which was supposed to be confidential. He was right to draw attention to that. However, he knows, as we all know, that due process is taking place. This matter is being investigated by the proper authorities. We can expect that when the investigation is complete appropriate action will be taken.
February 17, 1987

Apposite to that I would like to quote from an editorial in this week's issue of the Toronto Financial Times which refers to the leak of information which was supposed to have been confidential. The editorial writer says: "This doesn't detract from the good sense of the sale". That is the point for us to recognize and stress. This sale serves the interests of the people. With respect to the cash involved, I have different figures from his. I will quote from the February 23 issue of Maclean s magazine as follows:
The Government picked up $608 million in the deal, $102 million in cash which the telecommunications company had accumulated, as well as $488.3 million from the sale and an estimated $18 million in future income in cash.
These figures are different than mine. It seems to depend, in part, on what paper one is reading. However, I put that into the record.
I ask that the Member and the House see the wisdom of the sale which brings in cash for the taxpayers of Canada to partially finance programs which the Government has undertaken in their names. Finally, this is the kind of sale that the Government was elected to carry out. The Government was elected to privatize Crown corporations and reduce the Government's involvement in business. We are taking this step as part of that mandate. I trust that it will receive the approval of the House, as I am sure it will receive the approval of most Canadians. Indeed, if there is any criticism from the public it should be with regard to why we are not doing it faster and doing more of it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may, I will deal seriously with the issue of smallness. Of course, it is not the fact that the company happened to be small that is the concern. The concern is that the company happened, because of its smallness, to have to rely very heavily on bank loans in order to take over this company. In short, we have what is commonly referred to in commercial circles as a very highly leveraged company. Such a company has much less flexibility to face the ups and downs of the international business cycle than does a company which, as in this case, had over $108 million in reserves before the sale. That is the crucial difference.
With regard to small companies, it makes far more sense to encourage small companies to expand and to grow by themselves, thereby creating jobs, opportunities and exports, rather than to grow through quite ludicrous takeovers such as this. We have advocated that position quite widely.
My point in stressing the leak was to make what I think must be recognized as the ultimate criticism of this Government. While there are many Canadians who dislike the Government because of scandals, I can honestly tell the Hon. Member that it is my experience from talking to people in my constituency and elsewhere in Canada that those who put their faith in the Government have now withdrawn that faith, perhaps forever. I suggest they have done so because of a sense of incompetence in the Government, and this leak demonstrates such incompetence. I wish the Minister would get up and offer the House an apology for that incompetence in light of what has taken place.
Teleglobe Canada
Let me deal with the price. As someone who has worked for Maclean's, I hesitate to say that The Financial Post does have a slightly better grasp of financial figures than Maclean's. If we examine those financial figures in detail, there are two categories included in that $608 million. One category is dividends which could have been paid to the Government at any point. It is incorrect to say that they were received as part of the price. That reduces the price to under $500 million.
The second category is more questionable. It is a loan which was made by the Government to Teleglobe, which Memotec has taken over. Perhaps that should or should not be included in the price, but in any event, it does not mean that that money is suddenly available for the kinds of allocations to programs that the Member discussed. In fact, the $345 million I talked about seems to be the correct figure with respect to money available for allocation to programs.
Finally, the Member suggested that the Government was elected to sell our Crown corporations. I took part in the last election and I do not believe it was a promise that was either widespread or consistently made. In fact, in many cases, the opposite promise was made. Even if it was a promise, it was surely not to sell off our Crown corporations incompetently and at a low price, about which there is a sense of dishonesty. It just confirms to Canadians that the Government cannot be forthright.

Under public pressure, Mr. Speaker, I have decided that I too should speak for a few minutes in this debate on Bill C-38 which, as we all know, is aimed at privatizing Teleglobe Canada. First I should like to clear up any misunderstanding on the intentions of the Liberal Party about this question. Earlier the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault) took the floor and made a clumsy attempt to imply that the Liberals wanted to sell Teleglobe when they were in office, but now that they are in the Opposition they have had second thoughts and systematically denounce every single Government initiative. In my book, that is an exaggeration and a subjective interpretation of another Party's intentions. For openers, had the Liberals wanted to sell Teleglobe they would have done so. But they did not, and the best evidence of this is that Teleglobe is still there and still belongs to the Canadian people, and that it is the Conservative Party which is trying to unload this company. Besides, had the hon. Member for Argenteuil- Papineau wanted to be honest she could have said that, at one time, the Liberals did consider selling Teleglobe but changed their mind.
The philosophical approach of the Liberal Party of Canada is not to sell most Crown corporations, but it is not against that either. In fact we believe that selling Crown corporations is

February 17, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
something possible and even well-advised in certain cases. We study each case. For example, with respect to Canadair which the Government sold not too long ago, we were in favour of privatization for various reasons which I will sum up briefly. First, because Canadair was producing something, aircraft among other goods. We do not think that the Government has a role to play in replacing the industry to produce consumer goods. Then of course the sale rallied public support in Quebec because Bombardier was the buyer. Most Quebecers agreed with the sale, even including the labour union.
However the situation is altogether different in the case of Teleglobe. First of all, we are talking about a public utility. Teleglobe can be compared with a hydro power company or a public service such as highway and bridge maintenance. Teleglobe is a day-to-day service. Since this service has until now been provided by the Government-indeed, a benefit for Canadian consumers-we see no reason to change anything. Why fix something which runs smoothly? Everybody knows that in Canada you only need to lift the receiver off the hook to be able to talk to the person you are calling. Unfortunately it is not the same thing in all countries of the world. More particularly, international communications networks in Canada are extremely efficient. I simply cannot understand why the Government has decided to sell this company. It will now have to be regulated, yet there was no need for that before since it was a Crown corporation which set its own rates!

Why should something that is working so well be changed and given away at a price that is shamefully low?
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) stated in his budget speech of 1985 that the Government's philosophy on selling Crown corporations is that Crown corporations without a policy role could be dissolved. Why is the Government selling Teleglobe before the establishment of a national communications policy? It is in clear contradiction with the philosophy previously stated by the Minister of Finance.
[ Translation]
But the aspect which I find most revolting in the sale of Teleglobe is the price that was asked. To anyone prepared to listen the Government said that the company sold for $608 million, and that is what the newspapers have been reporting. But they have been somewhat more honest than the Government and delved for facts. This is how we learned that the Government is not going to recoup anywhere near $600 million from this sale. I will try to show that it is more like $300 million.
To begin with, consider the fact that Teleglobe cash assets now amount to $102 million. Of course we have been told that Teleglobe will give that money to the Government. Good gracious, how could it be otherwise? These $102 million belong to the taxpayers. So it seems normal to me that the Government would keep this money before the company is turned over to Memotec, the buyer. But no, Sir, this is not what they are going to do. They will hand over the $102
million to Memotec and then tell them: Give it back. This leaves under the impression that the government has obtained $102 million more, which is not the case. Moreover, Memotec will also have to return to the government $18 million in dividends. This means that the stated price of $608 million is now reduced to $488 million. That is not all. Teleglobe was indebted to the government to the tune of some $145 million. If that amount is deducted, we realize that the government will only collect $343 million for that sale. It is far from the $608 million announced. The government should refrain from boasting that it is a very good deal.
That is not a very good deal for Canadians. It is not a very good deal, it is a fire sale.

In addition, we should not only consider the selling price of $343 million which makes its a fire sale, we should also consider the benefits made by Teleglobe for the Government, hence the Canadian taxpayers. In 1985, Teleglobe paid dividends of $108,100,000 to the Government. In 1986, Teleglobe paid $80 million. This means that the corporation made handsome profits for the Government. It is easy to see that by letting it go for $343 million, we are deprived of returns of almost $100 million per year. With its anticipated profits the successful company, Memotec, must surely be laughing since-

Canadians. It was already provided for in Teleglobe's corporate plan. That is easy to understand since it is a company that has been very profitable for a few years.

What about the response to that sale? Let us see what those people who are the closest to the company, that is workers who go there every day, who earn their living in that company, think about the sale. I quote from the newspaper La Presse of February 12, 1987:
The communication employees union of Teleglobe, which represents 275 white collars of the firm, critized the sale of the company. The president of the national organization, Mr. Fred Pomeroy, said that the Conservative Government has sold out a profitable company-

-that the sale is not in the taxpayers' interest.
Of course the employees are right there, they are familiar with the operations of the company, and they know what they are talking about. They are against the sale. Since we are talking about past events, I might recall that when a Conservative Government was briefly in office for nine months in 1979 the Conservatives at the time were already toying with the idea of getting rid of Teleglobe. Ever since the employees have been asking themselves whether or not their heads were on the block as well.
Teleglobe Canada

I am saying that it is immoral to play with the emotions of the workers of a Crown corporation and to bring them up and down in a roller-coaster fashion. That is what has happened since 1979 in the case of Teleglobe.
Another item worth mentioning is the lack of involvement by the telecommunications carriers in this sale. They were not involved. In order to try to be involved they bid on the company. The involvement of the telecommunications carriers would represent a protection to the consumer, that is, a protection against a possible by-pass of international communications. By by-pass I mean that someone can call the United States and then have that call routed overseas through a communications agency located in the United States, in other words, by the American version of Teleglobe. Some 70 per cent of communications traffic in Canada could not be routed in this fashion. I refer to the traffic of Bell Canada and B.C. Tel which are federally-regulated companies and which cannot do that. What about the rest of the traffic, the 30 per cent that could be by-passed through the United States?

Mr. Speaker, I would like first to return to the comments of the mini-minister. He is asking that I regret calling him a mini-minister. I am quite ready to do that. I think he is right. We should refrain from personal attacks. By the same token, I imagine he will regret having interjected on top of his voice from across the House, which led me to label him in a way he did not appreciate. As a matter of fact, I was not attacking, I as the assailed was simply using defence.
Coming back to the issue of possible leaks, in answer to the Minister's question I would not take a legalisitic view of the matter as he does.
Actually, the Government is not before the courts fighting a charge of having caused leaks. It is rather that the media and Canadians across the land believe there has been a leak. It is in that sense I am suggesting the Government should clear the air. It is not my business, I am not part of that Government. But if I were on that side of the House, and rumours were circulating there had been leaks, I would feel the onus was on me to defend myself. I do not mean that in the legal sense, Mr. Speaker, but in terms of perception. So much so that we have been paddling about for some months in an atmosphere that does not reflect favourably on the Government in terms of perception, integrity and those matters, on which I have no intention of dwelling, because it is not the subject at hand.
That is why I say that, as reported in various newspapers, some Canadians believe that there must have been leaks for the shares to appreciate so quickly. The Government should feel the need to dispel any doubt concerning this matter.
While the Minister was shouting from his seat in the House, he asked me a question: Are you saying that there has been a leak? I could not certify that there has been one. But I hear everywhere that there could have been a leak. And I am quite concerned that there could have been a leak of this type from the Government. I did say there could have been- We have not reached the point where we know for sure that there had been a leak, but just the fact that the Canadian public may think that privilege information such as this may have seeped through the Government process is quite unacceptable. And especially in the interest of the governing party. This is why I tell Conservative Members to please disperse this cloud of suspicion for your reputation is at stake.
February 17, 1987

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: Since there are no more questions, on debate, the Hon. Member for Sarnia Lambton (Mr. James).

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to again address the House on this Bill. The Bill before us today is very important, and I am delighted to have the opportunity to clarify some of the points that have been made.
First, I wish to make mention of a point about no guarantees for employment, which was made by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) in an earlier statement or speech in the House.
I should like to bring to the Hon. Member's attention a press conference held on February 11 and attended by representatives of the company and members of the media. Mr. McKenzie, an official of the company, was asked the following question:
-will there be management changes at Teleglobe or any staff lay-offs, anything like that? Any surplus people?
Mr. McKenzie answered as follows:
I am glad you asked that question. Absolutely not. The Teleglobe, as we all know and as the Minister already indicated, is a very well run company... and his people are very, very good managers. One of the key points of our bid is that management is to be retained and all of the employees are to be retained. In fact, you know, that is the strength of Memotec-
He want on to say:
And we need the support of those people, the help of those people. We need those people to be motivated and enthusiastic towards what we are all trying to do. There will be absolutely no changes. In fact, we hope to create more employment through the synergies of the two groups. And that is the point we are trying to make, that we will create new employment opportunities, not decrease employment opportunities. I think this is a very positive story.
I think that answers the point raised by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor in which he attempted to cast suspicion.
The sale of Teleglobe is a good deal for the Government of Canada, for the employees of Teleglobe and, indeed, for all Canadians. The delaying tactics of my colleagues, especially those in the New Democratic Party, are not only unwarranted but unjustified. It is true that there is an ongoing investigation, as a previous speaker mentioned, but it is not an unusual occurrence. The Toronto Stock Exchange routinely investigates increased activity in any stock. The Minister is assisting in this investigation and is working very closely with the TSE to have the issue investigated. She is in constant contact with the Exchange and has requested her Deputy Minister to provide whatever details and assistance is necessary.
I am confident that the questions in the minds of the Opposition will be answered very satisfactorily and very directly. Surely the Opposition is not suggesting or accusing Memotec of any wrongdoing. It is necessary for us to allow the investigation to go forward, even as we move forward with the speedy delivery of the legislation to the appropriate legislative committee.
Teleglobe Canada
Once again I will go over the details of the bidding process and the sale to Memotec just to clarify some points. On November 19, 1986 the Minister announced that proposals would be received for the sale of Teleglobe based upon the comprehensive policy positions and the conditions of sale provided by the Government.
On January 9, 1987 CDIC received seven bids for the purchase of Teleglobe. A series of meetings between CDIC and the seven bidders were held to clarify points on the bids. Of course, these clarifications were needed by CDIC.
On January 27, 1987 the CDIC board met and considered the bids, including in its considerations a meeting with each of the seven bidders. At the conclusion of that meeting the management of CDIC was instructed to correspond with each bidder to allow them to consider their bids in light of the technical amendments to the draft agreement and the purchase of sale. In light of those changes, as per normal business practice, bidders were invited to refine, if they so chose, their proposed price for the purchase of Teleglobe.
On February 5, 1987 the CDIC board again met to consider the revised bids and determine its recommendations to the Government.
The next step is the crucial one, so I invite all Hon. Members of the Opposition to listen closely. The decision of CDIC was hand delivered by Mr. Paul Marshall to the Minister of State for Privatization (Mrs. McDougall) on February 8. The CDIC recommendations were taken to cabinet committee by the Minister on February 9 and a final decision was made by Cabinet at 5 p.m. on February 10, and the Toronto Stock Exchange was notified immediately.
These are the accurate details of the process. There were no difficulties with the bidding process and the utmost of secrecy was maintained until the date Cabinet made its decision.
It is important to remember that any of the six bidders could have closed the deal and had the financial backing to support the acquisition. The hue and cry from the Opposition about it being a leverage buy-out obscures one very important business point. To acquire a large and viable company such as Teleglobe, there are few companies in the country which could have done so without loans, and we were determined to keep Teleglobe in Canada.
I despair at the disparaging remarks the Opposition is making about the integrity and viability of Memotec. For the past few days in the House we have heard over and over again about the minnow that swallowed the whale. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what is wrong with that? Would the entire sale have been more digestible if we had sold Teleglobe to a major conglomerate? No, Mr. Speaker, I do not think so, because the Opposition would then have railed at the notion of too many assets in the hands of too few companies.
The second point I wish to make is to put an end to the Opposition's scare tactic that our Government is bent and determined, not only to privatize all Crown corporations, but

February 17, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
additionally somewhere along the line-opposition members have this mistaken notion-we are to move into the privatization of social programs. I cannot understand from where this would even come. It guess it is just rhetoric, something to say to fill in their 20 minutes.
Just to keep a balance on things, I want to take a moment to quote from the Minister's statement last Friday when she said:
Our policy is to better manage all Crown corporations, to wind down those entities which are no longer required, and to privatize on a case by case basis those Crown corporations where the public interest can be better served through private ownership with public regulation as and when required.
This point by the Minister must be remembered and addressed. It is our policy-and indeed it is sound policy-to examine individual cases. I can without hesitation assure the House that we will never move to privatize arbitrarily every Crown corporation, nor will we turn over to the private sector our existing social programs.
Let us take a minute to examine the Minister's statement in respect of private ownership and public regulation. Once again the Opposition has seen fit to muddy the waters. The new Teleglobe, unlike the old Teleglobe, will be subject to CRTC regulations for as long as the legislation remains in place. The five-year reassessment proposed in the legislation applies only to the monopoly situation, not to the CRTC regulations. This point has been mistakenly raised by the Opposition. It must be made very clear that rates offered by Teleglobe will be subject to CRTC scrutiny for many years to come.
Consumers will benefit from an average rate reduction on overseas telephone calls and from CRTC regulations in connection with the sale. Employees of Teleglobe Canada will benefit from a pension plan which is comparable to the current government plan. Additionally, they will have an opportunity to purchase equity in the new firm on extremely favourable financial terms.
Lastly, Teleglobe Canada will benefit by being able to pursue new opportunities, expand and grow under skilled private sector management. I would like to quote from a statement made by former Liberal Minister of National Revenue as reported in Hansard for May 28, 1984 while this House was debating second reading of then Bill C-25. He said:
The fifth part of the Bill-concerns CDIC's subsidiaries: Canadair Limited, The de Havilland Aircraft of Canada Ltd., Eldorado Nuclear Limited, Teleglobe Canada and, in the near future, Pecheries Cartier Inc. and Fishery Products
International Ltd.The clause deals with the relationship between the CDIC
and its subsidiaries, and the aim to change the status of those subsidiaries to private sector corporations.
Obviously the Official Opposition has changed its stand somewhat from that of 1984.
Similarly I quote the Hon. Member for Vancouver- Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) during the debate on second reading of the Canadair Bill. On December 1, 1986, he said:
We in the NDP are not necessarily against privatization. We are not saying in every case we should not privatize; we are saying you have to have sound economic reasons for it.
I have sat in this House and listened for the past few days to the Opposition's rhetoric and waffling. It seems the minds and opinions change to fit the issue of the day. I am reminded of Prime Minister Mackenzie King who also had a gift for speaking his mind clearly. He said:
Conscription if necessary, but not necessarily conscription.
I believe that in this case the sale of Teleglobe is not only a good deal but a great deal, and I believe the facts speak for themselves.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested in hearing the Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. James) describe how great is this Teleglobe deal. He notes particularly the observation of my friend from Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) about the possibility that the sale of some Crown corporations might be appropriate if there were sound economic reasons. Does the Hon. Member think that the reasoning here is sound?
To put it in the context of the Government's actions in the matter of regulation of various services in the federal area, which communications obviously is, what we see the Government doing is reducing the amount of regulation that has been applied in the past. What the Government is doing with Teleglobe is putting it into private area responsibility. The Government is taking out an international communications monopoly in Canada and turning it over to a private interest which, of necessity in the private sector, has other concerns than the public interest. First, it is obsessed with its own profitability. Every member of the Government would insist on that. Recognizing that that is the preoccupation of the privatized Teleglobe and the only control over the situation is staff regulation, what kind of assurance do we really have that a privatized Teleglobe will serve the public interest as it should?	.
We have a company which is, in the fullest sense, a utility in the communications area. Utilities tend to be monopolies. What has been recognized for 100 years by every economist, no matter how deep his or her dedication is to competition, is that monopolies need to be regulated. A Government that has no vision for creative regulation but wants to get out of it will take a utility and put it into the hands of private interests obsessed with their own profitability rather than serving the public interest. What kind of sound economic reasoning can one put forward for taking this vital communications utility and putting it into private hands, as the Government has done?

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased my hon. friend has asked that question. This sale gives a lot of opportunity for providing jobs. I know the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay- Nipigon (Mr. Epp) is very concerned about that, I say that sincerely, and I think that is very important. The employees are pleased with the transaction and I would think the Hon. Member would be very positive about that. I cannot recall seeing any statements that they were unhappy.
It has been said, and I think the Hon. Member heard me read a statement made by Mr. McKenzie at a press conference
February 17, 1987

on the situation and his belief about how important the employees will be to Memotec. I think the Hon. Member would have to agree that it has been written extensively in Canada, and I tend to believe it, that when employees have the opportunity to purchase shares in the company for which they work, have the opportunity to buy those shares at less than market price with interest-free money loaned by the company, it goes to excellent working conditions.
The rationale for divestiture of Crown corporations is to see them expand, grow and get into other areas not encumbered by the bureaucracy and the Government which really are not the best at being in business. The Hon. Member has a little trouble agreeing with me on that because the philosophy of the New Democratic Party is that the state runs everything.
In the May, 1986 Budget is this statement:
We expect the results of returning federal Crown holdings to the private sector, that privatization will reduce the size of the Government and leave room for more private sector initiative which will promote market competition and more efficient allocation of resources. It will improve company efficiency.
We can talk about a lot of things that are of value in this sale. It is important that we are doing good things for the people who work for Teleglobe and for those who will be able to work for the new important company with its new jobs and new opportunities.

subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with respect to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Sarnia Lambton, he has completely refused to answer the questions. There was not the slightest recognition of the fundamental difficulty that I put to him, namely, that the Government is backing away from regulation and making it easier for companies, whatever industry they may be in, to pursue their own ends rather than serve the public interest. Here we have a monopoly being put into private hands. What kind of protection is there for the public interest? The Hon. Member has not provided any of that. He has talked about other things. Let me challenge him again to respond. He said in passing that enhancement of competition was the goal of privatization. That is completely missing the point I was making. More particularly, the Hon. Member began by praising the increase in employment that will result from this sale. The Hon. Member will have to concede, surely, that there are no guarantees in the sale at all? The Hon. Member was forced to read a press conference and the statement by a principal of the new owner to defend of that. But there are no assurances. This is another of those cases of putting all sorts of things forward before the Canadian public without any assurance. That is the form of Government action far too often these days.

subtopic: MARINE TRANSPORTATION
MARINE TRANSPORTATION
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF TAX SYSTEM ON CANADIAN REGISTERED SHIPPING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada conducts over $50 billion worth of trade annually with countries other than the United States. This represents transportation fees of about $5 billion per year. Of that amount, less than 1 per cent is carried on Canadian ships. Twelve billion dollars of this trade is conducted with countries which have enacted legislation which will only allow cargo to be carried on ships of their national registry. Canada is the only country, to my knowledge, which does not allow tax exemptions of some sort or another on earnings from carriage of deep-sea cargoes. Even the United States and the United Kingdom allow companies to defer taxes indefinitely.
There are currently 120 ships owned by Canadian companies registered abroad which do not hire Canadians. These companies have expressed a desire to be able to operate out of Canada but state that their greatest hindrance is the present tax regime of the federal Government. In light of the fact that over 50 per cent of Canadian merchant seamen are currently unemployed and the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is bringing down his Budget Wednesday night, I would ask the Minister to make the necessary changes in the tax system so that these merchant seamen can be put back to work.

subtopic: PASSENGERS DESTROYING PASSPORTS ON BOARD AIRCRAFT-SUGGESTED DEPORTATION TO POINTS OF DEPARTURE
PASSENGERS DESTROYING PASSPORTS ON BOARD AIRCRAFT-SUGGESTED DEPORTATION TO POINTS OF DEPARTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on KLM Royal Dutch Airline flights 691 and 677 from Amsterdam to Toronto, a total of 22 illegal immigrants were apprehended by immigration officials last week. These individuals deliberately tore up their passports and other identification, thus committing an illegal act. If these individuals were legitimate refugees, there would be no need for them to destroy their documentation.
Under these circumstances we are not compelled by international law to admit such law-breakers into Canada. I strongly urge the Government not to give these individuals the right to land in Canada and to return them immediately back to their points of departure where they presumably had the legal right to be present since they boarded these flights. There

February 17, 1987
is no need to have such abusers stay in Canada at great cost to the Canadian taxpayer.
Canada must send out a clear message that those who cheat and lie will never be welcome in Canada. Moreover, the airlines are willing to co-operate as well.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT CORRECTIONAL SERVICES CANADA EMPLOYEES HAVE RETIREMENT ELIGIBILITY AFTER 25 YEAR'S SERVICE
REQUEST THAT CORRECTIONAL SERVICES CANADA EMPLOYEES HAVE RETIREMENT ELIGIBILITY AFTER 25 YEAR'S SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for almost fifteen years now the employees of the Correctional Service of Canada, more specifically correctional officers, have been seeking the right to retire after 25 instead of 35 years of service, as is the case for most public employees, with the exception of air controllers, the RCMP and the Armed Forces who may choose to retire after 20 to 25 years of service.
The federal Government must take into consideration the risks, dangers and stress associated with the duties of correctional officers. The extremely difficult working conditions of our correctional officers fully justifies retirement after 25 years of service.
Again recently the Minister said he had the intention of taking action on this matter. It is now more than time to do something and, hopefully, tomorrow's Budget should cover this measure of fairness with respect to our correctional officers.

subtopic: SHIPYARDS IN NEED OF CONTRACTS
SHIPYARDS IN NEED OF CONTRACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, six years ago some 14,000 people were employed across Canada in the shipbuilding and ship repair industry. Today that number has been reduced to about 5,000. We know that there is no free market in shipbuilding today but still we do not have a rational shipbuilding policy.
It is in the interest of all of us to maintain a healthy, modern shipbuilding industry to meet defence and commercial requirements. Canada is a maritime nation, heavily dependent upon trade, and we must not permit our marine industrial base to wither and fall. One preventive step is to impose a tariff on ships purchased offshore to work or to fish in Canadian waters. Another is an acceleration of the naval, Coast Guard, and government vessel procurement programs. Given fair competition, Canadian shipyards can do much to provide Canadians
with wide employment in shipyards and in hundreds of related industries. They need help and they need it now.

subtopic: REPEAL OF TARIFF ON BOOK IMPORTS URGED
REPEAL OF TARIFF ON BOOK IMPORTS URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Great Depression, two World Wars, a small and spread out population, recessions, inflation, and overwhelming intrusion and competition from the United States-none of these could kill Canada's book-publishing industry. However, collecting $36 million for the Budget through the Government's current imposition of the 10 per cent retaliatory tariff on books can. Not only is the tariff a tax on reading and a disguised form of censorship but it discriminates only against English-language books, and it has seriously harmed individual unit sales in the Canadian book industry. Publishers alone estimate they will lose $15 million by absorbing the tariff duty this year.
Some Canadian publishing houses are incurring losses as high as $30,000 a week in a gallant effort to hold on to their customers. They cannot continue much longer. With this loss of income, they have less cash available to publish Canadian works. I ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to take the opportunity to remove this regressive countervail tax on reading in his Budget tomorrow so that the Canadian book industry can once again flourish in Canada. As well, this was a poor policy response to the shakes and shingles countervail in the first place.

subtopic: WINNIPEG-STREET CROSSING PROJECT PRIORITIES
WINNIPEG-STREET CROSSING PROJECT PRIORITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 10, 1987, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) made a statement in this House concerning the proposed Waverley Street grade separation. This statement requires clarification. The Hon. Member suggested that a tragic accident might not have occurred had the federal Government followed through on a commitment made by his Government in 1984 to build an underpass at that location. This implication is false.
On March 27, 1985, the City of Winnipeg requested that government funding be reallocated from the Waverley Street grade separation to Keewatin Street which has a higher safety risk. Based on those facts the City of Winnipeg set the Keewatin Street crossing as top priority. A new application was submitted to the Canadian Transport Commission on November 27, 1986, by the City of Winnipeg, and is now
February 17, 1987

being considered. The promised funding is available and will be allocated based on the CTC's recommendation. In future the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry may wish to get his facts straight before condemning this Government's policy.

subtopic: FORT ERIE-LEAFLET DISTRIBUTED TO SALVADORAN AND GUATEMALAN REFUGEE CLAIMANTS
FORT ERIE-LEAFLET DISTRIBUTED TO SALVADORAN AND GUATEMALAN REFUGEE CLAIMANTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am reading excerpts from an informal translation of a leaflet given to Salvadoran and Guatemalan refugee claimants entering Canada from the United States at Fort Erie, Ontario. It says:

maintopic: FOR THOSE THOSE WHO BELIEVE THEY ARE REFUGEES FROM EL SALVADOR AND GUATEMALA

speechtext:
I.	The Immigration Officer has written a report that reads: you violated Canadian Law because you came across the border without bringing a passport and/or without bringing an immigrant visa.
9. The Minister's Permit is described in Section 37 of the Canadian Immigration Act. This section says that this permit can be annulled at any time by written order if you violate other Canadian laws or if the government decides you are not a refugee.
II.	For example, if you prefer robbery to work, you would spend time in jail, the government would revoke your permit, and would deport you to the United States.

subtopic: EIGHTH MERCURY AWARDS-SUCCESS OF ARGENTEUIL- PAPINEAU RESIDENTS
EIGHTH MERCURY AWARDS-SUCCESS OF ARGENTEUIL- PAPINEAU RESIDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my constituents of Argenteuil-Papineau and more particularly the residents of Lachute have had one more reason to be proud because, last Saturday when prizes were given at the Eight Mercury Awards organized by the Chamber of Commerce of Quebec, a young Lachute firm, Mobilier Form-D, received the Mercury Award given to a new business.

Congratulations to the shareholders and employees who can righfully be proud of this prestigious award which proves they had every reason to have faith in their own aspirations.
I also want to commend Mirabel's Nationair airlines for being nominated for the second consecutive year, IBM Canada
for deserving the 1987 Mercury Award, and the 71 Quebec firms which took part in this event.
To Quebec firms the Mercury Awards are what the Gemeaux awards are to artists, craftsmen and producers of the artistic and cultural community. subtopic: RAPE IN SHERBROOKE-REQUEST THAT AGGRESSORS BE IMPRISONED
RAPE IN SHERBROOKE-REQUEST THAT AGGRESSORS BE IMPRISONED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last May 26, a 26 year old woman was raped by three aggressors in Sherbrooke. There was so much violence used during this sexual assault that the victim has not been able to go back to work since. Last December 3, a jury unanimously found the three aggressors guilty and each one was sentenced last January 27 to five years in prison. However, the very next day, their case was appealed and they were set free. The reasons given were that the rapists had no criminal record, that they are young and that they are successful at school and in sports.
Mr. Speaker, the fact that her aggressors are out means that the victim, Dominique, has to be very careful about what she does and to try not to attract any attention. Her assaulters have been freed, they live in the same city as she does, Sherbrooke, which is not New York, and she is afraid of reprisals. If anyone should be hiding out of fear and shamed, it should be the aggressors, not the victim.
Mr. Speaker, I ask that the Minister of Justice review this case and that the appeal be heard as quickly as possible, and also that the aggressors be put in jail. If they are in prison, justice will perhaps be done more quickly in the case of this odious and serious crime.

subtopic: CONGRATULATIONS EXTENDED TO SOLIDARITY FUND OF QUEBEC FEDERATION OF LABOUR
CONGRATULATIONS EXTENDED TO SOLIDARITY FUND OF QUEBEC FEDERATION OF LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Solidarity Fund of the Quebec Federation of Labour for investing a few weeks ago over $200,000 in a high technology company located in Sainte-Foy, in my constituency, thus protecting and creating jobs. In addition, the Fund will invest $2 million in an office tower to be built in the Hull region at the end of the month.

February 17, 1987
It is the first time in North America that a union creates a fund whose major objective is to protect and create jobs by investing in the Quebec small business sector.
Once more, I congratulate the Solidarity Fund of the Quebec Federation of Labour and its president, Mr. Claude Blanchette!

subtopic: U.S.S.R.-RELEASE OF JEWISH DISSIDENT WELCOMED
U.S.S.R.-RELEASE OF JEWISH DISSIDENT WELCOMED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know all Members of Parliament will want to join in welcoming the announcement of the release of Iosif Begun, a leading Jewish dissident in the U.S.S.R. who had been imprisoned for supposed anti-Soviet agitation and propaganda. It is heartening that his release comes after the release of another 150 prisoners this month. We know that there are still several thousand prisoners of conscience incarcerated in the Soviet Union. We hope the Soviet Union will release many of them and that many of the Jewish dissidents will again find it possible to leave the Soviet Union.
We note and regret the fact that beatings and repression are still used against those from the Soviet Union who wish to demonstrate that such treatment of dissidents is the denial of human rights. Such incidents are sharp reminders that there is a great disparity in what is said about human rights by the Soviet Union and what actually happens to dissidents in that country.

subtopic: NATIONAL ACCOUNTS OPERATING SURPLUS
NATIONAL ACCOUNTS OPERATING SURPLUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the national finances we have turned the corner and can now see the light at the end of the tunnel. For the first time in many years the national accounts show an operating surplus. The third quarter results are now in for 1986 and reveal a small surplus, about $1 billion, over the preceding 12-month period.
Huge public debt service charges, the legacy of years of mismanagement by former Liberal Governments, still result in large over-all deficits, but the trend toward reduction has definitely been established. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is to be congratulated on his exemplary performance to date and urged to stay the course.

subtopic: JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II- CALL FOR GOVERNMENT TO HONOUR COMMITMENT
JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II- CALL FOR GOVERNMENT TO HONOUR COMMITMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has become painfully obvious that the Government has placed the Japanese Canadian redress issue on the political back-burner. When the current Minister responsible for multiculturalism, the Government's third, assumed his responsibilities, there was great fanfare that the Tories had finally found the ideal individual to address this most sensitive national matter. However, we have heard precious little since.
The Japanese Canadian community was promised before, during, and after the election campaign that the Conservative Government would conduct negotiations on redress and that a settlement would be worked out with the National Association of Japanese Canadians. Regrettably, both previous Tory Ministers ignored these two principles. Now we have the current Minister who is still occupied with obtaining cabinet approval on the process to follow.
This kind of action is simply an offensive response to what were clear promises made to a very important segment of Canadian society. It is about time that the Government finds its morality in dealing with Canadians. It should begin to honour its commitments, fulfil expectations which it created, and re-establish the people's confidence in their national Government and national institutions.
Otherwise, the Government should do everyone a favour and step aside so that Canadians can receive the kind of representation which they demand, rightfully deserve, and have not had for the last two and a half years.

subtopic: PURCHASE OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITIES FOR DEVELOPING COUNTRIES
PURCHASE OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITIES FOR DEVELOPING COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian International Development Agency was formed back in the 1960s to administer the major portion of Canada's official assistance to developing nations. New projects to be funded by CIDA include $310 million to the World Food Program for the next two years, $89 million worth of canola oil and technical assistance to India, $13 million worth of canola oil as food aid to Pakistan, and $40 million for the next three years to the Canadian Food Grain Bank which is primarily a humanitarian relief agency.
These development and assistance programs will involve more than $450 million worth of agricultural commodities, many of which originate in western Canada. These projects are good news for they not only provide help for the developing countries, but also for our own farmers whose commodities
February 17, 1987

form the basis for the assistance. The Government should be commended for its continuing support of these initiatives.

subtopic: HUNGER STRIKE LAUNCHED BY NON-STATUS INDIAN
HUNGER STRIKE LAUNCHED BY NON-STATUS INDIAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, six days ago Kevin Daniels started a hunger strike on the steps of the Saskatchewan Legislature. Mr. Daniels, a non-status Indian, has taken this extreme form of protest in order to draw attention to the plight of the indigenous people of Canada.
He hopes that his action will spur federal and provincial Governments to include land claims and self-government in the Constitution.
In a conversation I had with Mr. Daniels yesterday, he told me that the suicide of a close friend was the final reason that led him to go on a hunger strike. While I do not encourage anyone to undertake a hunger strike, it is a sad commentary on our society that somebody feels compelled to use this extreme form of protest.
The aboriginal people of Canada want to take control of their destinies. They are tired of welfare dependency, unemployment and high suicide, crime and alcoholism rates. They must be given the resources that were promised them so many years ago. They are tired of waiting.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, several months ago Canada Post introduced its latest contraption under the name supermailbox. This supermailbox could do almost anything and could guarantee mail delivery- should I say mail pick up-24 hours a day, seven days a week. That did not quite happen.
First, everyone and his cousin could break into the supermailbox with their bare hands. Then one's key could open personal mailboxes everywhere. Of course, this was part of the safety feature of the new supermailbox. Now people cannot break into these supermailboxes any more and there is no need to worry about the keys. The latest feature of the supermailbox is inaccessibility.
For four days last week my constituents in the Orleans area had no access to their supermailboxes because it snowed in Orleans and Canada Post could not keep up with the snow removal. Canada Post should install these supermailboxes where they really belong, in the junkyard.
