subtopic: TELEGLOBE CANADA REORGANIZATION AND DIVESTITURE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to spend a few minutes on the matter of the divestiture of Teleglobe. We must make clear to the House and the country that this is not a planned development of the economy. It is not a long-term decision by the Government that we must do these things in order that in five or ten years our economy will work well for the benefit of the citizens of Canada. Rather, this is a decision by the Government to divest itself of one of the central requirements of any country in relationships with the rest of the world. The Government's decision has been a matter of Conservative ideology. Instead of building a structure for the benefit of Canada, this is a general rejection of the notion that public enterprise should be used to achieve public policy.
The tradition in this country has always been for Crown corporations to be used for the needs of the country. Instead, we have the rejection of a traditional position taken by Canadian Governments, not only New Democratic or Liberal Governments, but Conservative Governments for many years. The history of Crown corporations in Canada shows that a good number of the Crown corporations which served Canada well were put in place by Conservative governments.
The Government holds the belief that Government should not be involved in any enterprise which can be carried out by the private sector, even if in the process it eliminates some of the public interests and policies which have been put in place. Instead of doing something to increase the economic development of the country, the Government is eliminating that possibility.
Let us look for a moment at the apparent reasons for what the Government is doing, besides the rejection of the fact that Crown corporations can be used to develop public policy, and besides the ideological basis for saying that the private sector should have the right to take as much profit as it possibly can from the country instead of allowing it to accrue to the people as a whole. The Government says it is doing this because it thinks the private sector will do a better job, or it needs to be done by the private sector. The Government seems to forget that we now have a company owned by the citizens of Canada which is being taken away from all of the citizens of Canada
Teleglobe Canada
and given to one small group. It is said that that is the market system, that it is now within the market. I fail to see the logic of that.
The Government keeps saying that this is one method of reducing the deficit. Although it may put $100 million or so into the coffers right now, over the long term it will increase the deficit because we will not have this well developed, profitable organization continuing to earn profits for Canada on overseas developments.
You must realize that this company has a certain amount of responsibility in the world as a representative of Canada. The Government should realize what it is doing. It is making into a private corporation an organization which has represented Canada in international communication affairs many times in the past and will apparently continue to do so. That was one of the responsibilities which Teleglobe fulfilled as a Crown corporation. It was Canada's representative on many international organizations, such as the Commonwealth Communications Committee which made decisions on our place in the world of communications. Will that mandate be fulfilled in the future by a private corporation, the aim of which is not necessarily to serve the best interests of Canada, but to serve its own best interests by earning as much profit as possible from its operations?
First, we must question the basis upon which the decision was made. We must question the plausibility of the reasons given for this decision being fulfilled by selling the assets of Canada in this way. This is exactly what has been done in Saskatchewan recently by the Government's friends there. The assets of that province have been reduced. The rating given to Saskatchewan by the financial institutions of the world has dropped from a triple A to a single A because the assets which were considered to be the base of the province were sold. Crown corporations are no longer provincial property and are not recognized as assets by the financial institutions of the world.
There are questions which will be asked when this Bill goes to committee. Those questions will deal with the authority and activities which Teleglobe will fulfil. We will ask who will fulfil these authorities when Teleglobe becomes a private institution.
Teleglobe Canada was created under the Teleglobe Canada Act and was mandated to establish, maintain and operate Canada's international telecommunications service and coordinate these services with those of other countries. Apparently the Government has decided to put the control that was ordinarily vested in the Government into the hands of a private, profit-oriented corporation.
The privatization of Teleglobe means that the Government is also relinquishing its control over our ability to contact other countries via telecommunications. The United States is the only other country in the world that depends upon the private

February 17, 1987
Teleglobe Canada
sector for such communications. Apparently, the Americans have a parallel communication network through their defence system. Since our defence communication system is not worldwide, and there will not be government control over these communications system, we may be unable to communicate with the world. Other countries such as Australia, New Zealand and Japan have government control over their international communications systems.
The Government has designated Teleglobe Canada as the Canadian signatory to the International Telecommunications Satellite Organization. Periodically, each of the signatory's ownership share is adjusted to conform with the percentage of their total use of the system and any other percentage that they elect to have within the agreement. If Teleglobe Canada is privatized and its purpose is not to serve Canadians but to make a profit from its operation, how can it fulfil its responsibility to Canadians within this agreement?
That percentage of ownership share in the telecommunications satellite organization is part of Teleglobe's asset. Therefore, one must assume that this share of satellite operation has been sold to a private corporation and the Government no longer has the ability to make use of those satellites for national purposes.
The corporation is also designated as the Canadian participant in the Commonwealth Telecommunication Organization, the purpose of which is to develop efficient operations of a Commonwealth communication structure. The operation of this global system is also apportioned to those in the Commonwealth who have taken part in the development of a global telecommunication system. The Government, through this Bill, is selling our interest in that telecommunications system. Yet, I wonder if the other nations of the Commonwealth who are involved in this organization were asked if they wanted as a partner a private corporation whose aim is profit rather than service to the Commonwealth or the country which it possibly represents?
Teleglobe Canada primarily functioned on behalf of the Government. We are told that it will continue to have this monopoly for five years and there is a commitment to reduce the price. When we consider the Government's previous policies in these areas, there is no assurance that the Government will not increase its subsidy to Teleglobe in the next five to ten years to keep it afloat. We know that the Government's mandate and responsibility is to assist in the development of a corporation.
We are told that the pension plan of the employees involved in this takeover has been settled. However, I was the member of our Party responsible for dealing with the Bill privatizing Canadian Arsenals. When I contacted employees of that organization I discovered that, although the Government thought it had settled that issue, the employees had quite a different opinion. In fact, that Bill was held up in committee for several days because the employees were dissatisfied with the proposal.
There is a retirement benefit equivalent to one-half the accumulated unused sick leave days up to March 31, 1981, with additional credits of five days per year of service after that date, calculated at the salary level in effect at the time of retirement. This is a commitment to people who are presently working for Teleglobe Canada. While government documents on this divestiture indicate that there has been some discussion on this question, there is no guarantee that this kind of commitment from the Government to the employees is safeguarded. While this may have been discussed, the unions and the employees should beware, because we know from other divestitures of Crown corporations that employees may lose in the long run unless they are very careful.
This divestiture also raises a question about the relationship of Teleglobe with the Department of Transport. The Department of Transport has supplied the use of cable ship icebreakers such as the John Cabot and others to Teleglobe on a reimbursement basis. This amounted to a cost of some $6.8 million a year. Will the Government be required to continue to give this kind of service to Teleglobe when it becomes a private corporation? Will we put at the service of Teleglobe, a private corporation, ice-breakers and cable ships, something which will cost and has cost the Canadian Government in the past as much as $7 million a year? Will the Canadian Government be reimbursed for the provision of these services? Or will they just be services to Teleglobe as have been delivered in the past to some extent?
These are the questions which have to be asked. Not only must we ask why we are selling it, we must ask how we will replace the services which Teleglobe has put in place for Canada, how much it has cost us and how much it will cost us in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I draw to the attention of the House one of the points made by the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), namely, the contrast he made between profit and service. His assumption is that if a utility is purchased by a private enterprise organization it is suddenly no longer a service corporation. I draw to the Hon. Member's attention the number of corporations in the country which have become known not only throughout Canada but throughout the world for the services which they render. I refer to Bell Canada, Consumers' Gas, Interprovincial Pipe Line and TransCanada Pipelines. Do members of the NDP not realize that if one wants to make a profit in private enterprise then one has to provide a service? If there is no service then there is no business and thus no profit. 1 belong to a political Party that believes fundamentally in the free enterprise system which will generate the most wealth for this nation that will ultimately serve all of its citizens. But we taper that belief in free enterprise with a concern that it is a legitimate role for Government to intervene to ensure that the distribution of wealth generated by a free enterprise system is fair and equitable. We taper that belief in free enterprise with the certain conviction that when it comes to providing goods and services to Canadians in equal measure, no matter where they live in this country, from time to time it is appropriate for Government to intervene to ensure that services are provided.
There are some very notable examples of this, such as the decision to establish what is now Air Canada. This was an example of a Government intervening to ensure that airline service would be available in equal measure, at a reasonable level, everywhere in Canada. That was a decision at a point in time when the private sector was not prepared to take it and, I would submit, is not prepared to take it today. There was a decision by a very famous Conservative Prime Minister, John A. Macdonald, to build a railroad from sea to shining sea because that act of Government intervention to ensure the railroad was built was part of the policy of the Government of the day to use the railroad, to use transportation, as a means of national unity. There are many examples, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was established, not because the private sector could not give us a broadcasting service in Canada, but because the Parliament of Canada believed instead that there was a requirement on the part of the Government to ensure that Canadians, no matter where they lived, would at least have a minimal level of service in both radio and television. So too was it part of the service, part of the needs of the nation, that Teleglobe Canada was put together to provide this country with a trans-Atlantic telephone service and to provide us as well with telex services.
What we have in this Bill is not an argument, there is not one shred of evidence that placing Teleglobe in private hands is going to give the people of Canada-because that is what counts in the final analysis-a better service or a cheaper service than is currently the case. What we have instead wrapped up in this Bill is an expression of a particular political
Teleglobe Canada
Party's ideology that in all cases, at all times, the private sector must provide goods and services in this nation.
1, for one, find it more than passing strange that the Government of Canada is seizing upon the assets of the people of Canada, profitable assets that belong to every man, woman, and child in this country that are returning an investment on behalf of the people to the Treasury of this country, and is privatizing those assets. Teleglobe Canada, a company until we pass this Bill, or until the Government majority passes this Bill, paid to its shareholders, and the shareholders are 25 million Canadians, $108 million last year and a similar amount the year before. Yet two years later, a new Government with a new philosophy, bound and chained like a slave to a doctrinaire philosophy no longer relevant in 1987, suddenly picked it up, lock, stock and barrel and, for $100 million, passed it back to the private sector with no guarantees to prevent a recurrence of the kind of problems with which we had to deal at a cost of $300 million a scant two or three years ago. That is what is frightening about the Government.
We are hearing about the sale of Air Canada. We ask why. The Government intelligently tells us: "Because". We ask: "Because why?". "Because the private sector should do it, of course". We are hearing about the sale of CN and we ask: "Why?". The Government says: "Because. Because the private sector should do it".
We do not have a national transportation policy any longer. We used to function on the notion that we would regulate services on the basis of public convenience and necessity. Now we have a new philosophy of fit, willing and able. If you have some dollars, Mr. Speaker, and the initiative, and you want to provide or eliminate a service, go right ahead. That is the philosophy of the Conservative Party.
The Government has said that the purpose of privatization is to put Teleglobe into the hands of the private sector. The Government has said that the company might benefit from private sector management. In announcing the Bill, the private sector is so confident of its ability to benefit this company that it has demanded that it remain in a monopoly position. It is the private sector if necessary but not necessarily the private sector. The scenario is that this company will function like a Crown corporation with a monopoly, with guarantees and with guaranteed profits, but the profits will go into the hands of the private shareholders, not the people of Canada who built the company. The profits will go into the hands of private individuals who will operate with public guarantees and with a government-sanctioned monopoly.
The Government has said that the purpose of privatization is to increase competition. For the next five years, during a time of growth and development in this particular field, again this company will have a government-guaranteed monopoly. One cannot be a half-way private-sector player. One cannot on the one hand talk about the virtues of the private sector, talk about freeing the entrepreneurial spirit, make the appeal to private initiative and competition, while on the other hand wrapping all that around a set of government regulations and monopolies and expect the people of Canada to swallow that line. I know the Speaker knows that. I know that if he were not constrained by the requirements of the Chair, the Speaker would be on his feet with his fists balled up demanding that this terrible piece of legislation be chucked through the door.

My hon. friend here asks why. It is because so far, the Government has put this debate within an ideological context. It says their reasons for selling Teleglobe Canada were that the private sector was more efficient than the public sector. It says that for the New Democratic Party it is only natural to demand that a corporation remain in the public sector. The Government has put all this into an ideological context.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with the matter a little more objectively. I would like to examine the sale of this company from a number of different angles. For instance, I would like to look at public policy reasons for maintaining Teleglobe Canada as a Crown corporation and for selling it to the private sector. That is one of the aspects.
Another aspect we should examine is the nature of this business. It happens to be a monopoly. How does one regulate a monopoly? How can one manage a monopoly in such a way that it serves the public interest? What is the best way to do it?
Another aspect of this matter is concerned with the profits and revenue of this company. Does the company have any financial problems? Who will benefit from its income?
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want to examine the sale of this company and the various aspects of that sale, because I think we should realize there are some questions. If the Government is so sure the company should be sold, it may be right. But can we ask a few questions, find out why the Government sold the company? If indeed we can ask questions, I suggest the Government must reconsider its approach. The Government will have to say: Yes, the company is now in the public sector and running smoothly. Why change anything if things are going well? Why fix something that does not need fixing?
Mr. Speaker, my first question was: Are there public political reasons why Teleglobe Canada should remain in the public sector rather than be sold to private interests? Are there such reasons, or are the Progressive Conservatives right when they say there is no need for this company to be in the public sector and that a private company can just as well serve the interests of Canadians?
What I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, is that Teleglobe Canada is our lever to implement the communications policy. It attests to our presence on the international scene. Mr. Speaker, there is a big world out there and we want to communicate with everybody. With Teleglobe Canada we can help Canadians keep in touch with the rest of the world. Such is the situation at this time.
February 17, 1987

But if we were to do what the Government is doing and ask that the company be sold, then it will become a private company and will want to make a profit. The company will have to be attuned to the requirements of the market, and there may be parts of the world with which Canadians may not find it profitable to communicate. So there will be pressure to do away with one aspect of our international communications.
As I see it, Mr. Speaker, if Canada is to remain open to the world and if Canadians are to be able to communicate with everybody, then it would be better if the company were to remain in the public sector because we can use it as an instrument to achieve public objectives and stay in touch with the rest of the world, not only with those countries where reciprocal communications may spell profit.
That, Mr. Speaker, is one public political reason why this company ought to remain in the public sector.
Another aspect to this question of public policy, Mr. Speaker, is that Teleglobe Canada speaks for Canadians on international organizations. Should Teleglobe Canada ever become a private company subject to the conditions of the private market, then it will speak for itself and defend the interests of its owner.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if it is to belong to international organizations then I think there is a possibility of conflict of interests-the interests of the Government of Canada and of the people of Canada, and the interests of a private company working to make a profit and represent the interests of its owner.
In that case, Mr. Speaker, I think we will have to express serious reservations about the sale of Teleglobe Canada. Indeed, the way things are now, the company operates as an instrument which can represent all Canadians on international organizations, but once it has been sold we will have to find some other way to be represented on those organizations. We will also have to find a way to gather information on the international telecommunications industry to be able to represent our own national interest, our interest in international organizations.
I will give you an example. For years, the oil industry in this country belonged to the private sector and was in fact dominated by private companies. These companies gave the federal regulator information on Canada's oil reserves. For years they said we had plenty of oil and we could sell the oil we had. We were dependent for that information on those companies. After a while, in a matter of years, the companies changed their minds. They said: Watch out, the oil is running out. And we had the oil crisis. Mr. Speaker, in that situation we depended on the private sector for information that was essential to the interests of this country.
I think the same situation could apply in the telecommunications industry. When we depend on a private company for our knowledge of the industry, we may not get the information we need to understand the industry and safeguard our interests.
Teleglobe Canada
Mr. Speaker, the second aspect of this question I want to look at is the nature of the telecommunications industry. This corporation is a monopoly and it dominates the industry, of course, and my question is as follows: Is it more efficient to regulate a monopoly through ownership or through regulation? I think there are two ways of managing a monopolistic industry. One way is to have a regulatory agent who can look at the company and say: O.K., do this or do that, take this or that direction. That is one way. The other way is to buy the company or go along with the company in the public sector, and simply be able to tell its managers: This is Canadian policy, and we want you to respect that policy and to follow it, because you are the owners of this company and you can do that under our economic system.
Mr. Speaker, today we can control this industry because we own it. However, the Government is going to change the situation and put us into another where we will have to depend on a regulatory system. Mr. Speaker, the trouble with a regulatory system is that sometimes the regulators get too cozy with the industry they are supposed to regulate. It is like policemen on the beat. They're supposed to be there to control crime, for instance, the sale of drugs. Policemen patrol the streets to get rid of this kind of activity. Sometimes, however, they may accept bribes and forget their responsibility to the public. They become friends with the people selling the drugs. They are no longer regulating the situation, they are part of it. I think this could happen in industry. Instead of regulating the industry, the regulatory agent starts representing the interests of that industry.
Mr. Speaker, we now have a good system for managing the telecommunications industry in our country, which is a monopolistic industry, and why should we change it? If the system works, why change the system?
The third point I want to look at is the matter of profits and income generated by Teleglobe Canada. Mr. Speaker, it is common knowledge that Teleglobe is a profitable operation that is earning income every year. So why sell the corporation and transfer it from the public to the private sector when it is making a profit? The Government has said it will use the profits of this sale to reduce the deficit. But, Mr. Speaker, if we continue to own Teleglobe Canada we can expect to make a profit every year. The company can contribute to put money in the public treasury for years to come. It is difficult to understand why the Government would want to sell a successful company. I have the impression that this Government is a little bit ashamed that a public sector company should be so profitable. The philosophy of this Government is that the private market is the most efficient vehicle to do just about everything, and it has very little respect for Crown corporations. They often say that a Crown corporation simply cannot operate the way a private company does.
Mr. Speaker, I am forced to conclude that a successful Crown corporation is an embarrassment to this Government. It would rather not have Canadians look at this example as

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE JUDICIARY ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PROCESS FOR SCRUTINY OF FEDERAL JUDICIAL APPOINTMENTS
speechtext:
The Judiciary
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of undertaking negotiations with the provincial Governments to establish a process for the parliamentary scrutiny of federal judicial appointments made under Section 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867, in order to ensure that in making these appointments, the Government is guided by the highest standards of conduct.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to move the motion with a view to establishing a system and process of parliamentary scrutiny for all federal judicial appointments. The purpose of that is to reinforce public trust that all judicial appointments are of the highest calibre, and that in making those appointments, the Government is guided by the highest standards of conduct.
During the 1984 election campaign, the appointment of lawyers to the bench was a major issue. In particular, the former Prime Minister Trudeau, before he handed over power, entered into an agreement with the then Prime Minister, Mr. Turner, which called for a number of people to be appointed to various positions, including a number of people who were to be appointed to the bench. At that time, the then Prime Minister, Mr. Turner, who is now the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra, made those judicial appointments. In doing so, he touched off a controversy that is still going on.
I draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, as recently as last month the appointment to the Court of Appeal of the Province of Manitoba made in the person of the former Premier of the Province of Manitoba, Sterling Lyons. There was a controversy around that appointment and the method of that appointment. The law union of Ontario had some comments on that, and I will be referring to those comments later in my remarks.
As a result of the concerns that were raised during the election campaign, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made a statement in the House on September 5, 1985. In that statement he dealt with a package of reforms that included an experimental program for the parliamentary scrutiny of Governor in Council appointments. At that time the question of judicial appointments was excluded from that parliamentary scrutiny. At that time the Prime Minister indicated that the Minister of Justice had the question of judicial appointments under active review. Unfortunately, that review is apparently still going on, and as yet we have not heard the results.
The motion that I put before the House today is in the hope that the Government will move on this, complete the review, and take some action here.
I do not wish to leave the impression that I am in any way questioning the competence of our judiciary or the high calibre of our judges. I do believe that we have a judiciary of a very high calibre in this country and that we are well served. At the same time, I share the concerns that were expressed in 1984 by the Chief Justice when he said that the public is entitled to be reassured that our judges are appointed on the basis of merit and legal excellence alone.
I also share the concerns expressed by the Canadian Bar Association about the independence of the judiciary in their

February 17, 1987
The Judiciary
report of August, 1985, where they indicated that the existence of political influence in judicial appointments could undermine public confidence in the judicial system. That is what I am trying to accomplish with this motion. I am trying to make sure that public confidence in the judicial system is not undermined, but is in fact bolstered by a new system of appointments.
You are aware, Mr. Speaker, as are Members of the House, that the Government has a number of different ways of making federal judicial appointments. There are five different statutory federal courts: the Federal Court, the Northwest Territories Court, the Yukon Court, the Tax Court, and the Supreme Court of Canada. In addition to that there are appointments made under Section 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867. Those are appointments that are made by the Governor General to the superior, district, and county courts in each province, except the courts of probate in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. As I indicated, those appointments are made under Section 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867.
In practice the process that is followed at the present time calls for the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) to recommend to the Governor in Council via the Cabinet persons who are to be considered for judicial appointments. Of course, the appointment of a Chief Justice rests with the Prime Minister. In practice, in following that process, the Minister of Justice does not appoint someone off the top of his head. There are people in his Department, in fact in the office of the special adviser to the Minister of Justice, who gather suggestions from across the country on these judicial appointments. The suggestions may come from you, Mr. Speaker, they may come from me, or from anyone in Canada or abroad, for that matter, as to who might be appointed as a judge by the Governor in Council.
After those suggestions have been vetted and a tentative choice has been made, the candidate's name is normally submitted to the National Committee of the Judiciary of the Canadian Bar Association to receive their opinion and evaluation. Normally, that committee comes back with an opinion that the suggested candidate is either well qualified, or not sufficiently qualified.
During the last federal election campaign there were two or three appointments made to the bench, the ones that touched off the controversy, where there was no request made to the Canadian Bar Association for its input. That is what put the fat in the fire and caused the public concern to be raised about whether the process was one which ensured that the best individuals were appointed to the bench, or whether the process in place is one that is being manipulated in some way.
Over the years there have been a number of different proposals for reform. There was one made by the Tremblay Commission in 1956. There was another made at the Constitutional Conference in 1971. There were further proposals made in 1978 and 1979. The Canadian Bar Association made recommendations in 1985. Quebec made some changes to their procedure in 1978.
However, the Americans have a process which is most interesting, that is, a process whereby a committee of the Senate vets the recommendations made by the President of the United States. In scrutinizing the suggested appointments, that committee can recommend for or against the appointment, or it can delay the matter. It is this type of review that I am suggesting we should be undertaking in this country. That review would be open to all Members of Parliament and all members of the public, but it is not the kind of review the Department of Justice, or probably the Minister of Justice, would like to see. I think we will hear from some government supporters today who will oppose this idea because they do not think it is the way to go.
As well, it is not the kind of procedure the Bar Association would like to see established, but it is a procedure which would be open to the public and would give us a solution, at long last, to one of the major concerns of Canadians in the last election campaign. It would reinforce public trust that all judicial appointments are of the highest calibre and that in making those appointments the Government is guided by the highest standard of conduct.
For those reasons I urge the House to adopt the motion and to put in place a process for a new method of parliamentary scrutiny of judicial appointments.

Referring to the Order in Council review process as proposed by the Hon. Member for York-East, he is suggesting that we have a system which would resemble the present system of reviewing other Order in Council appointments. By and large I think the system has worked well over the last year or so. It has provided Members of Parliament with an opportunity to air a grievance when there is a controversial Order in Council appointment. Most appointments are completely overlooked by Members. They look at the names and the names do not mean anything to them, or they inquire in various areas and find out that the individual is qualified, and they do not proceed any further.

On the other hand, there are the "Dalton Camp" variety of appointments which lead to controversy and to some questioning in committee. That is healthy as well because it at least gives parliamentarians on all sides of the House an opportunity to raise the grievance at committee. That is good for two reasons-first, it is good accountability, second, it gives the Government an opportunity for second thought. Whereas the Government may proceed with a controversial appointment, if it knows just before doing so that it will be subject to scrutiny by the Order in Council appointment process, perhaps it would have a second look at it and say, "We had better not bring this before the parliamentary committee because it will raise a considerable amount of attention; let us not appoint this controversial individual" or "this less than totally qualified individual", as the case may be.
For that reason alone I believe the quality of Order in Council appointments is bound to improve. I think it has improved over the last year in which the Order in Council process has existed. As the Hon. Member for York-East said, it does not exist for the judiciary and for other areas as well.
In closing I should like to make a few comments about veto power for the parliamentary committee. I do not think the committee needs veto power in the case of judiciary appointments. I suppose it could be tried for some processes, but I do not think this would be a good place in which to try it. The fact that Parliament would have a method of raising a grievance would be good. However, there are some 60 or 64 Order in Council appointments which deal directly with the House where a parliamentary committee should have veto power. Those concern the appointment of the Chief Electoral Officer, the Clerk of the House of Commons, the Official Languages Commissioner, and so on. The report of the McGrath Commission recommended that there be a veto process for those individuals. I believe that would be healthy. We could start there. Depending on how it works-and presumably it would be less partisan because we are dealing with officers who report to the Speaker of the House-we could decide later about expanding it elsewhere if it were necessary and desirable. However, it would be premature to say that it would be necessary at this point in the case of judicial appointments.
Having said that, however, I whole-heartedly agree with the motion of the Hon. Member for York-East. Indeed it is a valid concern to be raised. As the Hon. speechtext: What about Ian Deans?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE JUDICIARY ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PROCESS FOR SCRUTINY OF FEDERAL JUDICIAL APPOINTMENTS

It was absolutely shameless. When the Liberal Member stands up and lambastes the Conservatives for their excesses of patronage, I would very gently remind him that one of the reasons his Government was turfed out of office was that Canadians got sick and tired of the Liberals' excesses of patronage.
With respect to the proposal before the House, I can think of no body which is more important and essential in terms of the shaping of many of the most fundamental values and aspirations of our country then the highest courts of the land, the courts of appeal and the Supreme Court of Canada. We have as a Parliament adopted a Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The final word with respect to the interpretation of that fundamental document rests not in our hands as elected Members, but rather in the hands of those men and women who are appointed under Section 96 of the Constitution Act to
federal judicial appointments. It is up to those men and women to determine, for example, what is or is not demonstrably justifiable in a free and democratic society under Section 1 of the Charter.
What are the limits that we as a society are prepared to accept on fundamental rights and freedoms? At the present time these judicial appointments, these appointments to the highest courts of the land, are made solely by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in the case of the Supreme Court of Canada and solely by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) in the case of others. In some cases, these appointments are made following consultations with the Attorney General of the province in question. In other cases, even the minimal courtesy of consultation with the Attorney General of the day is ignored. I would remind you, Mr. Speaker, of the recent appointment of Sterling Rufus Lyon, former Premier of the Province of Manitoba, to the Manitoba Court of Appeal. Mr. Lyon was appointed to that very important position in the federal judiciary without any consultation whatever by the federal Minister of Justice with his provincial counterpart, the Attorney General of the Province of Manitoba. That kind of arrogance and insensitivity in an area as fundamental as this is surely unacceptable. That total lack of consultation, that appointment of a Tory crony, would not be possible if the motion of the Hon. Member for York East were adopted.
We have had some experience in this Parliament with the parliamentary review process into federal appointments. As a member of the Standing Committee on Human Rights I participated in a process, which admittedly was a flawed process, an engineered process, but nevertheless gave us the opportunity to ask a few questions of appointees who appeared to have been appointed solely on the basis of partisan political connections to the Government of the day. What is interesting is that one individual knew that he would have to undergo this kind of scrutiny and it was sufficient to cause him to withdraw his name as a member of that tribunal. That is of considerable significance and another reason for supporting the motion of the Member for York East.
I am reminded of the attempts of former President Richard Nixon in the United States to appoint to the highest court of the land in the U.S., the United States Supreme Court, individuals who were clearly unqualified. Had it not been for the fact that the Senate of the United States in its judiciary committee said no to the appointments, those individuals would be sitting on that court possibly still today, patently unqualified.
I mention the Supreme Court of Canada and the vital importance of an opportunity for parliamentary review of appointees to this highest court in the land. I do this in view of the fact that there is a vacancy at the Supreme Court of Canada level due to the tragic death of former Justice Julien Chouinard, and I urge the Government to appoint a woman. There are a number of qualified outstanding jurists who would fill this vacancy at the Supreme Court of Canada with distinction. I think of people such as Madam Justice Claire

L'Heureux-Dube of the Quebec Court of Appeal. There are a number of others. We must send out a message that equality in Canada is a reality at all levels, including the highest court in the land.

Member for York East for bringing this important question before the House of Commons today and to urge all Members to support it, particularly in recognition of the fact that it merely calls upon the Government to consider the advisability of undertaking negotiations. These judges are making decisions that will shape the future of this land for decades to come. It is essential that we as Members of Parliament, in the highest court of the land play a role in ensuring that we know just who the men and women are who are occupying these vital positions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like those who have spoken previously, I want to say a few words on behalf of this motion which, I believe, is not only in the best interests of the people but is an extension of a principle of accountability that has already been established in this Parliament under the leadership of this Government. We have had our first experience of parliamentary review of major appointments. This has been the first Parliament with a Government prepared to risk a public review of its nominations and appointments. There is more accountability under this Government than the people of Canada have ever known before.
The motion before us recommends to the Government and the House that we take a major step forward. I certainly commend the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) for the leadership that he has characteristically shown in putting before us this initiative, which I hope will receive the support of the House and will lead to the action the Hon. Member anticipates.
I support the motion because of the authority and scope the judiciary has come to gain in recent times. Members of the judiciary have always enjoyed great authority and power, but because of the very nature and development of the law, they are now in a position which is unparalleled and unprecedented. They are now not only interpreting and applying laws but, at various levels, they are making laws because their interpretations are the binding authority by which laws will be implemented in, and applied to, society. It is surely reasonable and essential that appointments to positions of that magnitude have the approval and support of the elected representatives of the people of Canada.
The quality of our judiciary has certainly come a long way. I can recall beginning my working life as a newspaper reporter who spent part of his time covering police court hearings, as they were then called. I remember one magistrate whose sole professional qualification for being on the Bench was his years as a retail merchant. It was a patronage appointment made by
The Judiciary
a previous Liberal Government in Ontario. However, the partisan nature of the appointment is not the crucial thing, however much we may want to dwell on partisanship from one point of view or another. The important thing was that it was then possible for a person to occupy a position on the Bench without professional qualifications.
I doubt that is possible today, and rightly so. However, we want to see that not only professional qualifications are demanded but that we be satisfied as a Parliament that the person receiving a judicial appointment, certainly at the highest levels, will be one whose professional qualifications are superior, who has views on society compatible with those of the majority of Canadians, and who can interpret the law in a way appropriate to the traditions of Canada and the thinking of the majority of Canadians today.
I do not want to take up the full time allotted to me because I know there are other Hon. Members who wish to have a say on this important and significant motion. However, I would point out very briefly that an argument could be made against this motion that, contrary to the intention of the mover, it would discourage some people from being willing to assume high judicial office because they would then have to face, terror of terrors, Members of Parliament.
I find it extraordinary to think that any other official appointed to any other post of authority under this Government would be subject to parliamentary scrutiny except one kind of official, namely, a member of the judiciary. This, I submit, without any slight to members of the judiciary, is surely to build an unnatural and indefensible wall around the judiciary. If it was justified at any time in the past, it is not so now because of the very nature of our society as an increasingly open society and because of the very nature and scope of the law today applied to more and more instances and experiences of life. It is therefore mandatory that the people who are prepared to take this office are also prepared to be examined for it, to explain themselves and to justify their views. I think that would be far better than having persons appointed to the Bench now and then having their reputations impugned by Members of Parliament in certain situations without their having the opportunity to reply to charges or insinuations that Hon. Members might make.
I believe that rather than discouraging persons who would be qualified and suitable and indeed eminent members of the Bench, this motion will assert that anyone who is prepared to mount the Bench, to interpret the law and to apply the law to society is one who is prepared to face the representatives of the people over whom the judge will preside as a member of the judiciary. That person will put his or her views to the test and will be all the more effective a judge as a result.
I am very glad the Hon. Member for York East has brought this motion to the House. I along with other Hon. Members certainly hope that it will come to a vote and that it will be an affirmative one.

speechtext:
I would object to the provinces finding their way into the appointment process unless there was some reciprocity.
Let me turn to the central point, that there ought to be parliamentary scrutiny of federal judicial appointments made under Section 93 of the Constitution Act. I want to found my remarks on the report of the Canadian Bar Association committee on the appointment of judges in Canada issued on August 20, 1985, and very well received. The report deals with the question of parliamentary scrutiny and rejects it, as the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) may know. The report says that Parliament should not play a role in the selection or appointment of federal judges. It is neither necessary nor desirable for the legislative branch to be involved. It is contrary to the Canadian tradition for the appointment of judges to be subjected to a congressional-type process of public examination and review.
Those who have spoken before me in this debate have referred to the American experience. However, the American Constitution is fundamentally different from ours. The executive in this country derives its legitimacy from the support of the House of Commons. The executive in the U.S. derives its legitimacy from the fact it is directly elected by the people. The same applies to the U.S. Congress. In that sense Congress can claim an independent responsibility for the judiciary. The executive nominates, but in a system of checks and balances Congress has some role to play in the appointment of judges. In our system the executive controls the House of Commons. If it did not, it would not be able to hold on to power and make appointments. Therefore the idea that the American experience is somehow irrelevant to us is totally inappropriate. It is a different kind of system.
I would also assert that nothing that has happened in the appointment of Canadian judges, over recent history in any event, justifies parliamentary scrutiny. People can make the point, as some have done, that a bad Government might make bad appointments and the House of Commons might be able to find enough gumption or independence to do something about it despite the fact that the majority is controlled by Cabinet. However, I do not think it is the nature of the Opposition in this House to play a constructive role, nor does it have a constitutional responsibility for the appointment of judges, a system which, according to the Canadian Bar Association and 1 think according to most Canadians, has been working quite well and serving the national interest quite well. In saying that I do not want to be taken as having said that the system for appointing judges is perfect. I just have to look at the Canadian Bar Association report, because it does not just endorse what we do now, it recommends a number of changes
February 17, 1987

designed to enhance the appearance of independence, the process, and the amount of public involvement in the process.
I want to deal now with one of the recommendations in this report with which I do not agree. I want to return to the point made from the floor by the Hon. Member for York East. 1 do not know if I have his ear, but in this report a recommendation is made that provincial attorneys-general ought to be consulted in the federal appointment process. I took it from the first few lines of the resolution that provincial Governments would participate. My friend is making the point that the role of provincial Governments in his resolution is only to change the Constitution and not deal with the appointment of judges. However, this report recommends that attorneys-general be given a role in the process of appointing federal judges.
1 want to ask the same question in that context that I asked in connection with his resolution. If provincial attorneys-general are to be given a role in the federal appointment process, and I oppose that, then the federal Government should be given a role in the provincial appointment process. After all, the justice field is shared between the federal and provincial Governments and this one-way street suggestion made by the CBA overlooks the fact that the federal Government has a great interest in the competence and qualifications of all judges in the system. The federal Government relies on provincial Governments because that is the way the Constitution is designed. The provincial Governments, for their part, have to rely on the federal Government for the way in which federal appointments are made and the quality of the people appointed. If I were to be engaged in a change which would bring a provincial perspective to the federal appointment process I would want to see it move the other way as well. However, as I say, I have reservations about both of them.
On the whole I do not think the history of federal appointments has shown any justification for scrutiny by Parliament. If parliamentary scrutiny is to be applied to judicial appointments it will have the effect of politicizing them in a way they have not been to date because of the role the Opposition plays in this House. That role, I would argue, unlike the U.S. system, is to politicize and object. It is not similar to the role of the U.S. Congress in making the American system work.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate this evening on Motion No. 43 presented by the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway), which concerns the appointment of judges. Mr. Speaker, to help Canadians understand what the debate is about this evening, perhaps I may explain that the Hon. Member for York East would like us to start negotiations with the provincial Governments in order to establish a process for the parliamentary scrutiny of federal judicial appointments.
Mr. Speaker, although I agree with the substance of the motion, I must object to it, unfortunately, and I have two specific reasons for doing so.
The Judiciary
First of all, the Hon. Member is suggesting that we relinquish federal authority to appoint judges to the provincial governments. This may be going a little too far, because today, when such appointments are made, there is already a certain amount of consultation that goes on with the provinces, but I think we should be very careful how we consider any proposal to undertake negotiations with the provincial governments with respect to appointments.
My second point, Mr. Speaker, which may be rather interesting, is the question of parliamentary committees. I may remind my hon. friend that not long ago at the caucus meeting in Laval about two weeks ago, Quebec Members made a proposal in this respect which I think deserves our attention and which is substantially similar to what is being suggested by the Hon. Member for York East who would like to see something different in the procedure for judicial appointments.
Mr. Speaker, since we are talking about the appointment of judges, why could we not study the proposition of the Quebec caucus to the effect that a selection process be put in place, a kind of board for these appointments which could examine the qualifications of people likely to be appointed to the bench? For example, Mr. Speaker, this board could be made up of people like the chief justice of the court involved, where the new judge is to be appointed, a Bar representative, an official designated by the Government, and probably somebody to represent the government of the province where the whole thing is taking place. The board could hold hearings for all individuals duly qualified for and interested in an appointment, then it would prepare a list of applicants with the required qualifications to be appointed to the bench and present this list to the Government which would select the appointee.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind you that this process- exactly as I just described it-this process of a committee or a group including the various categories of people mentioned has now been in existence in Quebec for about ten years, and every time an appointment has been announced there have been negative comments concerning the individual appointed to the bench.
I think that my colleague and I agree on the principle, we differ only on the way to go about it. I doubt whether a parliamentary committee would really be the best way to make these appointments to the bench. I believe that individuals who are already in this field-Bar members would qualify for this, I think-would be in an ideal position to assess the qualifications of people applying for judgeship, just as much as the chief justice of the court involved, and the federal or provincial governments could appoint a representative who would sit on this appointment board.
Mr. Speaker, this is the position that I wanted to outline in this House, but I still want to congratulate the Hon. Member for his interest in the issue of judiciary appointments and add that I also believe that we should find another method for making these appointments.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE JUDICIARY ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING PROCESS FOR SCRUTINY OF FEDERAL JUDICIAL APPOINTMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my friend, the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway), moved:
That the Government should consider the advisability of undertaking negotiations with the provincial Governments to establish a process for the parliamentary scrutiny of federal judicial appointments made under section 96 of the Constitution Act, 1987, in order to ensure that in making these appointments, the Government is guided by the highest standards of conduct.
No one can disagree with the view that, in order to maintain the public trust with respect to judicial appointments, those appointments must be of the highest calibre. There also is no disagreement that in making those appointments the Government must be guided by the highest standards of conduct. No previous Government has taken as many steps as the present one to improve the practice of consultation with the provinces, the Bench and the Bar. Furthermore, as the Hon. Member knows, the constitutional negotiations currently under way by the Province of Quebec include the question of that province's role in the appointment of the three judges from Quebec who were required to serve on the Supreme Court of Canada.
Referring specifically to the motion presently before the House, it is my belief that it would have exactly the opposite effect to that intended by the Hon. Member for York East. By subjecting prospective judicial appointees to the scrutiny of the parliamentary committee comprised of political partisans, the public trust in the calibre of appointments could conceivably diminish. While it cannot be predicted with any certainty in advance, review by a parliamentary committee may well reduce the quality of candidates willing to accept an appointment. Furthermore, there is a risk that anything a prospective appointee says before that committee will be interpreted by some group or another as raising a reasonable apprehension of bias with respect to the judicial proceedings over which that appointee subsequently presides.
Another shortcoming of this motion is that it would send the wrong signal to the provinces with respect to their own appointment process involving provincial court judges. The federal Government is, quite appropriately in my view, looked upon for leadership in matters of this nature. By adopting this Bill we would be telling the provinces that they, too, should screen prospective judicial appointees in this manner. I do not think we should do that. To date not one province or provincial official has advocated vetting judicial candidates through a parliamentary committee. Nor, for that matter, has any leading member of the Bar advocated such an approach. In fact, it was expressly rejected in 1985 by the report of the Canadian Bar Association committee on the appointment of judges in Canada and, subsequently, by the Canadian Association of Law Teachers.
I really do commend my colleague from York East for his consideration and his upholding of the way the Government and any Government makes appointments, be they judicial or otherwise. I feel very strongly that because the report of the
Canadian Bar Association on the appointment of judges in Canada rejected such a recommendation, we must take a very long look at this.
This motion complements my friend's Private Member's Bill, Bill C-259, which he tabled about one year ago which failed to win the support of this House. That Bill called for the parliamentary scrutiny of judges appointed to the so-called Section 101 courts. I did not support Bill C-259 when it was tabled, and my views with respect to parliamentary screening of judges have not changed. I feel very strongly that competence comes first. Competence must always come first in appointments, and the public must have trust in the Government with respect to judicial appointments which must be of the highest calibre.
There is no disagreement that, in making those appointments, the Government must be guided by the highest standards of conduct. Our courts and the people appointed to the judicial boards must be of the highest standard possible. I know that the people of the Government, as well as all the people of Canada, would certainly demand and expect to have competence come first. In that regard, Mr. Speaker, I did not support Bill C-259 when it was tabled and, with respect to parliamentary screening of judges, I have not changed my views.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT-WINNIPEG CANADA PACKERS PLANT LAYOFFS-RETRAINING OF WORKERS. (B) REQUEST THAT DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER HELP SITUATION IN WINNIPEG.
EMPLOYMENT-WINNIPEG CANADA PACKERS PLANT LAYOFFS-RETRAINING OF WORKERS. (B) REQUEST THAT DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER HELP SITUATION IN WINNIPEG.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the packing industry for the killing and processing of meat products has played an important role in the economic wellbeing of the City of Winnipeg and the Province of Manitoba for many years. It is not surprising that I asked a question about the possible demise of the Canada Packers plant and the very serious effects that this would have on the City of Winnipeg and the Province of Manitoba.
Some years ago, Swift Canadian, which had employed hundreds of workers in their packing plant in Winnipeg, closed down and left workers unemployed. Now we are facing the lay-off of 450 workers, many of whom have worked for
February 17, 1987

Canada Packers for many years. This lay-off will take place in April of this year.
There is a distinct possibility that another 550 workers employed by Canada Packers will lose their jobs, as the company is considering very seriously the closing of its whole packing plant in the City of Winnipeg.
How did this happen? In 1986, the federal Government made an initial grant of $865,000 to facilitate the establishment of a hog killing and processing plant in Neepawa. That plant opened in September. When the Government made the announcement that it would make this grant available so that a plant which could kill and process hogs could be established in Neepawa, the union representing workers in Winnipeg warned the Government of the dire consequences of that action. They pointed out that there was very little increase in the number of hogs that are processed in the Province of Manitoba and predicted that if the plant opened in Neepawa it would have very serious adverse effects on the Canada Packers plant in Winnipeg.
In December, 1986, unfortunately the warnings of the union were proven correct. Canada Packers announced the closure of its beef kill and processing operation at its Winnipeg plant. As I already mentioned, 450 workers will lose their jobs in April.
The existing plant in Winnipeg is about 50 years old. The company also announced the real possibility of closing its entire Winnipeg plant in 1988, unless it decides to build a new modern processing plant. The company made it clear that it would not proceed with the building of a new plant without financial assistance from the federal and provincial Governments.
Most of the workers who will be laid off in April, and the rest of the 1000 workers who would lose their jobs if the whole plant closes, have worked for that company for many years. It will be very difficult for many of them to find other work.
I call on the federal Government to act in co-operation with the company and the provincial Government to assist in financing the building of a new Canada Packers plant in Winnipeg.
Discussions are also taking place about expanding the Burns plant in Winnipeg, which would give work to 200 more workers. If the Government is considering financial assistance to that plant, I urge it to require the Burns company plant to give first opportunity for employment in the expanded plant to workers who have been or may be laid off by Canada Packers, as one of the conditions for receiving the grant.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bud Bradley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: EMPLOYMENT-WINNIPEG CANADA PACKERS PLANT LAYOFFS-RETRAINING OF WORKERS. (B) REQUEST THAT DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER HELP SITUATION IN WINNIPEG.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) I would like to elaborate on the action being taken to help the workers who are to be laid off from the Canada Packers plant in Winnipeg.
Adjournment Debate
First, the Minister wants to underline that he shares the concerns of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) with respect to the future of these workers. Like him, the Minister believes that every effort must be made to help these workers through the difficult adjustment they face. The Minister also agrees that the best results will be achieved if the company, the employees, the federal Government and the provincial Government work together to put in place the assistance the workers need.
To this end, intensive discussions took place throughout January between Employment and Immigration Commission officials, company and union representatives, as well as with senior officials of both the provincial Department of Labour and the Department of Employment Services and Economic Security.
On behalf of the Minister I am pleased to be able to report that agreement has just been reached with all parties to begin work immediately on a joint adjustment action plan. The federal Government will participate through the Commission's Industrial Adjustment Service, and the Province of Manitoba will do so through its Employment Adjustment and Technological Change Program, a Manitoba jobs fund initiative.
Activity will be carried out by two committees. One, composed of company and union representatives, will address the needs of the 400 hourly-rated workers; the other, composed of company and non-union employees, will address the needs of the 75 salaried workers.
Committee costs will be shared equally by the company, the province and the federal Government. Both committees will be chaired by the same independent chairperson to be chosen by the committee members themselves. The Commission and the Province of Manitoba have each identified representatives to assist and advise the committees. The types of assistance which the committees can consider recommending are many and varied. They can range from retraining, sessions on resume writing or job search techniques, to job counselling, vocational testing or financial counselling.
This is an urgent situation and one in which none of the parties intend to let the grass grow under their feet. It is also an excellent example of federal, provincial and private sector co-operation.
Although the circumstances are difficult, the Minister is confident that through the joint efforts of Canada Packers, the United Food and Commercial Workers International Union and both levels of Government every possible resource will be tapped and organized to help the workers prepare for, and find, new jobs.

subtopic: FISHERIES-MARKETING OF FRESHWATER FISH-SENATE COMMITTEE REPORT
FISHERIES-MARKETING OF FRESHWATER FISH-SENATE COMMITTEE REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I asked of the Minister of Fisheries and Ocean (Mr. Siddon) was on October 30. Thus some time has passed since the questioning took place. However, it does not really matter

February 17, 1987
Adjournment Debate
since the question was about the marketing of freshwater fish, which problem has been with us for many, many years. In fact, it has been with us since the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation was established. I am afraid it will be with us for some time to come unless action is taken quickly by the Minister of Fisheries. I realize that cod and tuna are in the limelight; but I think that white fish and trout should also have their day in court.
The problem with FFMC is that it has a monopoly. The fishermen are not allowed to sell fish to any other body than the FFMC. No competition in the industry is allowed. It is forbidden to Canadian citizens to become buyers, sellers or dealers of freshwater fish in the parts of the country to which the FFM Act applies. New marketing ideas cannot be tried because of the FFMC. Fishermen in my part of the country, in the Northwest Territories, feel that they have been neglected by FFMC, which tends to concentrate on the Lake Winnipeg area.
We produce a premium product that ought to be sold for premium prices. But we fear that our top quality fish has been used in some way to subsidize the lower quality Manitoba production. That may or may not be true. But unless there is competition, and people are allowed to try new marketing ideas, we will never know for sure.
I can assure you that the state of the NWT fishing industry is desperate. It depends on continued subsidies to keep it going, about $.5 million a year from the territorial Government alone' That was not the case when private enterprise was in the business of selling fish. Now there is bureaucratic regulation rather than an open market system.
The Senate report was a very thorough study. Under the Hon. Jack Marshall, the Senate committee travelled widely throughout the freshwater country. They went to Hay River in the Northwest Territories, received the advice of territorial government fishermen's organizations and a wide variety of the general public. The local press contained a number of articles, and the report was favourably received. This was an illustration of the Senate doing its job. There was excellent work done by this conscientious Senate committee. The committee came up with a series of good recommendations. In my opinion, they pulled the punches a little bit. They could have been more straightforward, but they did a good job.
The committee's recommendation 13(b) was probably the most important in that report. That recommendation recommended the licensing of private fish dealers, and the return of private enterprise to the fish business. People are out there who are ready and willing to do this once the authorization has been given. Not long ago I was talking to some Chinese friends who told me that white fish that are salted in a special way command a price in Hong Kong of about $8 a pound. They would like to get into the business of specially salting this fish. Presently the fishermen receive a few cents a pound for the product, so there is a new market that needs to be tapped.
We need authorization by the Minister so that this licensing can take place, and private enterprise can be brought back into the business. It is my considered opinion that unless private enterprise and competition is not brought back into the northern fishery, that fishery will perish. Of that there is no doubt.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) has asked for the Government's response to the interim report on the freshwater fisheries that was prepared by the Senate Committee on Fisheries. I applaud the concern shown by the Hon. Member for his constituents and for freshwater fishermen throughout the West. His knowledge in this field is unquestioned in the House, and the Minister thanks him for his input on issues of this nature.
To date that committee has published only the first of a series of interim reports entitled The Marketing of Fish in Canada. Although the report is entitled marketing of fish, it contains some 20 wide ranging recommendations. They deal with such issues as resource management, federal, provincial and territorial matters, the mandate of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation, and, of course, marketing.
The Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation was established in 1969 at the request of provincial Governments for the purpose of bringing order to the marketing of freshwater fish products, and increasing returns to the approximately 3,500 fishermen involved in these fisheries.
Since 1969, the Corporation has been successful in meeting the objectives of its mandate, as indicated in the annual reports of the Corporation which have been tabled in the House each year.
The Corporation continues to enjoy the support of the participating Provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Ontario, and the Northwest Territories. It also enjoys the support of the vast majority of the fishermen in the Corporation's territory. Officials in the Department of Fisheries and Oceans have examined the recommendations with great care.
The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) has written to the distinguished Senate committee Chairman giving his views on the report. The Department is currently in the process of implementing many of the recommendations contained in the report. Subsequent reports dealing with the Atlantic and Pacific fisheries will receive the same attention and scrutiny, so that, as the Hon. Member mentioned, we can consider cod, salmon, white fish and trout.

subtopic: NORTH ATLANTIC TREATY ORGANIZATION-LIBERAL PARTY CONVENTION RESOLUTIONS
NORTH ATLANTIC TREATY ORGANIZATION-LIBERAL PARTY CONVENTION RESOLUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you are well aware, the present Progressive Conservative Government is firmly committed to peace and to nuclear disarmament. That
February 17, 1987

is not a unilateral nuclear disarmament but a multilateral verifiable nuclear disarmament. It is only a multilateral verifiable nuclear disarmament which will ensure that we can continue to maintain our Canadian democratic values and institutions, to maintain the rule of law, to control our own country, to prevent war, to deter aggression, and to settle disputes peacefully.
This is why we in Government have in the past and will continue in the future to support NATO and co-operate with the United States in the defence of North America.
The Canadian Ambassador to NATO, Mr. Gordon Smith, told me last week that our commitment to NATO is the reason Canada is consulted by the United States in all negotiations which take place with a view to bringing about nuclear disarmament. The United States consults all its NATO allies. It consults Japan, it consults Australia, but it does not consult Switzerland or Sweden. It no longer consults New Zealand, since New Zealand decided to ban American ships from its ports on the basis that they might be carrying nuclear weapons or might have some sort of nuclear power. It is the basis of the right to be consulted and the fact that we are consulted which rests on our commitment to NATO.
While we may not have the ability to negotiate or the influence to change everything we would like to change in the way of the nuclear problems of the world, we have the power to be consulted, and we are consulted because of the commitment to NATO. Perhaps, because of that, we can shift the approach taken to negotiations for nuclear disarmament.
If we decided to leave NATO or, for that matter, unilaterally declared Canada to be a nuclear free zone, we would be forfeiting the ability to influence in some way the negotiations for nuclear disarmament or for other kinds of conventional disarmament, perhaps the consultations on the first use of nuclear weapons in Europe, or the decision to use nuclear weapons first, before anyone else does. We would be forfeiting the right to consultation. It makes no sense for us to forfeit that right or to get out of NATO, nor does it make any sense for us unilaterally to declare Canada a nuclear free zone. Whatever happens in a nuclear exchange between the United States and the Soviet Union, whether or not we are a nuclear free zone will not save our hides.
Because of that it is disturbing to hear that the Liberal Party of Canada, in its most recent convention, adopted a resolution which called upon Canada to become a nuclear free zone. It was distressing to hear members of the Liberal Party saying that it was now official policy of the Liberal Party that Canada be a nuclear free zone.
It is interesting that the former defence critic for the Liberal Party indicated that if that happened no longer could American warships call in Canadian ports, and that we would virtually be in the same position as New Zealand. It is interesting to note that the Liberal Member who said that is no longer the defence critic for the Liberal Party.
Adjournment Debate
It is disturbing as well to hear one Member of the Liberal Party, the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nunziata), say that world peace is more important than membership in NATO. You and I know, Mr. Speaker, that NATO is synonymous with world peace. In fact, it has guaranteed peace in Europe and peace, as far as we are concerned in Canada, for the last 38 years. Of course it is not surprising when members of the New Democratic Party advocate that we get out of NATO or advocate a unilateral declaration of a nuclear free zone in Canada because that has been part of the NDP policy since 1969. It is not surprising when we hear New Democrats talking about it. But it is surprising and disturbing when we hear the Liberal Party talk about this same thing, particularly when Liberals have been such strong supporters of NATO and a multilateral and verifiable nuclear disarmament all these years yet now suddenly they are changing.
When it is time for the next election and the New Democrats and Liberals are asking for your support, Mr. Speaker, I hope that you will consider very carefully the things they have been saying in the last few weeks and months about this issue of nuclear disarmament, NATO and about their commitments to NATO. As you well know, if we elect a Government which is not supportive of NATO, is not supportive of multilateral and verifiable disarmament, we are going to take ourselves out of the game of playing a role in the disarmament negotiations and risking at the same time Canadian democracy, values and institutions under the rule of law. That, I hope, you will bear in mind at the time of the next election, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the fifth time in the last five days that I have had the honour to stand and address you in my place. I only wish the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) could have been present. She alluded a short time ago in my constituency to the fact that she never sees me in the House and never hears me speak. This would have been a good opportunity for her.
I recall too clearly the confusion surrounding the resolutions regarding NATO that came out of the Liberal Party Convention in Ottawa in late November. Of course, I share my hon. colleague's concern about the kind of signal this sent to our allies. However, rather than dwell on what the Liberal Party stands for, let me repeat what the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) said in this House on December 1, 1986. He said:
__anything which substantially weakens Canada's commitment to NATO would
indeed weaken the western alliance and not contribute to the fulfillment of peace.
This statement, Mr. Speaker, parallels what the now Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) said when he was Prime Minister, that if we are going to have any influence in working toward world peace we must first of all fulfil our commitments to our NATO allies.

February 17, 1987
Adjournment Debate
This Liberal resolution on NATO was raised at a Standing Committee on National Defence meeting on December 2 last where the Associate Minister was asked what the Government's reaction was. I think the Associate Minister's answer bears repeating. He said that the present Party in power which forms the Government of today supports NATO completely and absolutely.
Finally, let me say that Canada as a founding member of NATO has a long history within this important organization,
and we see no reason to alter our strong support and commitment to it now.
